templates.title: Slow queries against their own fingerprint's p90
templates.subtopic: per-group percentile baseline (PERCENTILE_CONT), time windows, anti-noise thresholds

sections.scenario: A platform team that runs dashboards and transformation jobs on a cloud data warehouse wants a daily list of queries that ran unusually long. A single threshold ("anything over 60 seconds") is useless: a nightly transformation always takes minutes, while a dashboard tile that suddenly takes ten seconds is a regression. So each query is compared with its own history: queries with the same normalised text share a fingerprint (query_hash), and a run is slow if it took far longer than that fingerprint's recent 90th percentile. The query log records the total elapsed time and how long each query waited in a queue for a busy warehouse.
sections.problem: Using query_history, write one PostgreSQL query that returns query_id, query_hash, warehouse_size, exec_ms, baseline_p90_ms, baseline_runs: one row per outlier query that started on {{report_date}} (UTC), ordered by query_hash, then exec_ms descending, then query_id. A query's execution time is exec_ms = total_elapsed_ms − queued_ms. The baseline of a fingerprint is the set of its runs with start_time in [{{report_date}} − {{baseline_days}} days, {{report_date}}); baseline_p90_ms is PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) of their exec_ms, rounded to 1 decimal place, and baseline_runs how many there are. A fingerprint with fewer than {{min_runs}} baseline runs is not evaluated. A query is an outlier if exec_ms > {{factor}} × p90 (compare with the unrounded p90). {{status_rule}} {{size_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{queries}} rows; the production table has hundreds of millions, partitioned by day.
sections.assumptions: The table is a simplified, hypothetical query log; real query-history views carry many more columns (compilation time, bytes scanned, partitions pruned) with their own documented definitions. Fingerprints, times, the factor and the thresholds are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: exec_ms excludes queue time; the baseline is exactly the previous N days, half-open, without the report day; PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) per fingerprint with the run minimum inclusive; strictly greater than factor × p90; UTC days with the last second of the report day in and the next midnight out; failed runs excluded everywhere (Hard+); per-size baselines and the absolute excess (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss drift, normalisation, incremental percentiles and alert precision.

clarifications.q: Why subtract queued_ms?
clarifications.a: A query that waited for a busy warehouse is a capacity problem, not a slower query. This report is about the query's own execution.

clarifications.q: Does the report day's own run count in its baseline?
clarifications.a: No. The baseline is the previous {{baseline_days}} days, ending at midnight UTC at the start of {{report_date}}.

clarifications.q: Which percentile definition?
clarifications.a: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9): linear interpolation between the two nearest ranks, as in PostgreSQL.

clarifications.q: Is a run at exactly the window start in the baseline?
clarifications.a: Yes. The window is half-open: the start is in, {{report_date}} 00:00:00 is not.

clarifications.q: Is exactly {{factor}} × p90 an outlier?
clarifications.a: No. It must be strictly greater.

hints: Compute exec_ms once in a CTE, with the status filter, so the baseline and the report day agree on what a run is.
Aggregate the baseline with PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY exec_ms) and COUNT(*), and put the run minimum in HAVING.
Join the report day's runs to the baseline on the fingerprint; the inner join drops fingerprints that were not evaluated.
followups: The dashboard team says a p90 over 7 days hides a slow drift: the baseline drifts up with the regression. How would you detect a gradual slowdown as well as a sudden one?
Two runs of a fingerprint scanned 10 MB and 40 GB because of different filter values. Is execution time the right thing to compare? What would you normalise by?
Run this daily over a table with hundreds of millions of rows a day. How do you avoid recomputing every fingerprint's percentile from scratch, and is an approximate percentile acceptable?
Product wants the list to page someone. What precision would you need, and which additional guards (absolute excess, repeated occurrences, warehouse changes) would you add before it pages?

rules.ask: A fingerprint has a few runs that take 20 times longer than the rest. What does that do to a mean-and-standard-deviation baseline, and why does the problem use a percentile?
Your percentile function differs from PERCENTILE_CONT. On 11 runs, which value does each return, and when could it change the answer here?
A query waited 40 seconds in the queue and executed in 2. Is it a slow query in your result, and should it be?
Your baseline is a moving window. Does it include the report day's own runs, and what does that do to a sudden regression?
The same fingerprint runs on an extra-small and a large warehouse. What happens to the baseline if you mix them?

templates.title: Listing consumers per month, trial versus paid
templates.subtopic: range (interval) joins, precedence within a group, first-ever events, COUNT DISTINCT by month

sections.scenario: On a data marketplace, providers publish listings (shared datasets) that consumer accounts can query directly, without copying the data. A consumer gets access through an entitlement: a free trial for a limited period, or a paid subscription. Providers want a monthly report per listing: how many distinct consumer accounts actually used it, how many of them were paying, how many were still only trying it, and how many were new. You have the provider-side consumption log, one row per query a consumer account ran against a listing.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, listing_id, consumers, paid_consumers, trial_only_consumers, new_consumers: one row per month (the first day of the UTC calendar month of query_ts, as a date) and listing with at least one counted consumer, for months {{from_month}} through {{to_month}}, ordered by month, listing_id. A query counts only if an entitlement of the same listing_id and consumer_account covers it: starts_at ≤ query_ts < ends_at, where a NULL ends_at means open-ended. A query is paid if a paid entitlement covers it, otherwise trial. In a month, consumers is the number of distinct accounts with a counted query, paid_consumers those with at least one paid query, and trial_only_consumers the rest (so the two add up to consumers). new_consumers counts the accounts whose first counted query on that listing, ever, falls in that month. {{coverage_rule}} {{history_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{queries}} queries and {{entitlements}} entitlements; the production log has billions of rows across thousands of listings.
sections.assumptions: The entitlement model, account names and listings are hypothetical and simpler than any real marketplace's (no usage-based pricing, no regions, no organisation hierarchy). The consumption log here is the provider's own derived table, not a product view.
sections.criteria: A half-open interval join from queries to covering entitlements; one row per query with paid precedence; consumers counted once per month and listing; paid plus trial-only equals consumers; new consumers from the first counted query over all history (Very Hard) computed before the month filter; uncovered queries and the provider's own queries excluded; UTC months with boundary seconds correct; deterministic order; can discuss cohorts, the cost of the interval join, organisations and small-count privacy.

clarifications.q: A consumer's trial ended on the 12th and their paid subscription started the same moment. Which do they count as for that month?
clarifications.a: Paid. Any paid query in the month makes the account a paid consumer for that month, and it is not also trial-only.

clarifications.q: Is a query exactly at ends_at covered?
clarifications.a: No. Entitlements are half-open: starts_at is covered, ends_at is not.

clarifications.q: Does an uncovered query make an account "new"?
clarifications.a: No. Only counted queries exist for this report, including for "new".

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines the month?
clarifications.a: UTC, the session time zone.

clarifications.q: Should a month with no counted consumers appear with zeros?
clarifications.a: No. Only month-listing pairs with at least one counted consumer.

hints: Start from queries joined to the entitlements that cover them. One query may match two entitlements, so collapse back to one row per query with BOOL_OR(kind = 'paid').
Then reduce to one row per (month, listing, account) with BOOL_OR(paid); every column is a count over that grain.
Compute each account's first counted query per listing before filtering to the report months.
followups: The provider asks for trial-to-paid conversion: of the accounts whose trial started in a month, how many had a paid query within 30 days? Sketch the query and the cohort definition.
The consumption log is billions of rows. The interval join to entitlements is the expensive part: how would you make it cheap, and where would you precompute?
The same consumer organisation uses several accounts in different regions. How would you count organisations, and what would you need from the provider's own data to do it?
Providers must not learn what consumers queried, only that they used the listing. Which fields of this report are safe to show a provider, and how would you protect a listing with only two consumers?

rules.ask: You count distinct accounts per month. If the provider asks for a quarterly figure, can it be the sum of the three monthly numbers?
Is your coverage check inclusive at ends_at? Which query in the sample would it wrongly count?
You used a ranking to pick one entitlement per query. Which one wins when a trial and a paid entitlement both cover it, and is the choice deterministic?
Is the first query computed before or after you filter to the report months, and which account would be wrongly new if it were after?
A query has no covering entitlement. Where does your left join drop it, or does it still count?

templates.title: Active, time-travel and fail-safe bytes per table per day
templates.subtopic: date spine (generate_series), interval states as of a snapshot, running totals

sections.scenario: On a cloud data platform, deleting or overwriting data does not free storage at once. Removed data stays recoverable for the table's time travel retention period and then, for permanent tables, spends a further period in fail-safe, a recovery window that only the platform operator can use; both are billed as storage. A finance team that keeps seeing storage bills grow after large clean-ups wants a day-by-day view per table of how many bytes are active, in time travel and in fail-safe, rebuilt from a log of storage changes.
sections.problem: Using table_settings and storage_events, write one PostgreSQL query that returns day, table_name, active_bytes, time_travel_bytes, failsafe_bytes: one row for every table and every day from {{start_date}} to {{end_date}} inclusive, ordered by day, table_name. Each row is the state at the end of the day: the snapshot instant is the next midnight UTC, and an event counts if event_ts is before it. ADD adds bytes to active storage. REMOVE takes bytes out of active storage at event_ts = t; those bytes are then in time travel during [t, t + retention_days days), in fail-safe during [t + retention_days days, t + retention_days days + F), and gone afterwards, where F is 7 days for a PERMANENT table and 0 for a TRANSIENT one (this exercise's rule; check current docs). A table with no events yet has zeros. {{kind_rule}} {{drop_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{events}} events; production has millions of tables, so the answer must not depend on a fixed list of names.
sections.assumptions: Table names, sizes and retention values are hypothetical. Real platforms track storage per micro-partition and can share partitions between clones; this exercise uses one simplified lifecycle per removed chunk, and the 7-day fail-safe and the zero for transient tables are stated as this exercise's rule. Retention is constant for each table.
sections.criteria: A spine of every day and every table; end-of-day snapshots with strict event_ts < snapshot; removed chunks classified by half-open intervals [t, t + retention) and [t + retention, t + retention + F); fail-safe only for permanent tables, retention 0 handled (Hard+); events before the range included; DROP converted to the active amount with a running total (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss retention changes, byte-day billing, incremental computation and how to explain a delayed storage drop.

clarifications.q: Is a removal at exactly midnight in the previous day's row?
clarifications.a: No. The snapshot for a day is the next midnight, and an event counts only if it is strictly before it, so an event at midnight belongs to the day that starts then.

clarifications.q: Bytes removed with 1 day of retention at 2026-09-10 00:00 — where are they at the snapshot 2026-09-11 00:00?
clarifications.a: In fail-safe (permanent) or gone (transient). Time travel is [t, t + 1 day), so it has just ended.

clarifications.q: Do I need a row for a table on days before its first event?
clarifications.a: Yes, with zeros. Every table, every day.

clarifications.q: Are events before {{start_date}} relevant?
clarifications.a: Yes. They set the active total, and data removed earlier may still be in time travel or fail-safe.

hints: Build a spine of days with generate_series and their snapshot instants, and cross join it with the tables.
Turn every REMOVE into one "removed chunk" (table, t, bytes); then each state is a conditional sum over chunks with t < snapshot, using t + retention and t + retention + F as the boundaries.
Active bytes at a snapshot are the ADDs before it minus the chunks before it.
followups: A table's retention is raised from 1 to 30 days halfway through the month. What happens to data already in time travel under your model, and what would you need to know to model it properly?
Finance wants the report in byte-days (or GB-months) to match a monthly bill. How do you integrate the daily snapshots, and what is lost by sampling once a day?
Over millions of tables, the cross join of days and tables is large and mostly unchanged. How would you compute this incrementally each day?
A clean-up job deleted 40 TB yesterday and the team expected the bill to drop. Using this model, write the explanation you would send them, with dates.

rules.ask: You walk events with LAG/LEAD. How does a removal from twelve days ago still affect today's fail-safe bytes in your query?
Why does a transient table never show fail-safe bytes, and when would you choose one for a staging table?
Is the end of time travel inclusive or exclusive in your query, and what does a removal at exactly midnight do on the snapshot one retention period later?
Your spine has one row per day. What does it cost for a million tables, and what would you materialise instead?
A table is dropped and then restored within its retention. What happens to the bytes in your model, and what would the log need to record?

templates.title: The fewest warehouses for a day of scheduled tasks
templates.subtopic: interval partitioning (minimum resources, lowest-free assignment), schedule expansion, DAG start times

sections.scenario: A data team runs its scheduled transformation tasks on dedicated virtual warehouses, and wants each task run to have a warehouse to itself so that runs never compete for compute. Warehouses cost money while they run, so before reorganising the schedule the team wants to know the fewest warehouses that would carry every run in a period, and a concrete, reproducible assignment of runs to warehouses that it can compare with today's. As on many schedulers, a task whose previous run is still going does not start a second overlapping run; that scheduled run is simply skipped (this exercise's rule; check current docs for a real scheduler's options).
sections.problem: Implement plan_warehouses(tasks, horizon). Each task is (task_id, size, first_start, every, duration, after), times in whole minutes. A root task has after == () and is scheduled at first_start + k × every for k = 0, 1, 2, … while the scheduled minute is < horizon. A run occupies one warehouse of the task's size during the half-open interval [start, start + duration); a run that starts before horizon runs to the end even if it ends after it. A scheduled run is skipped if the task's previous run that actually ran is still running at that minute (its end is after the scheduled minute). Then take all runs in order of (start, task_id) and give each one the lowest-numbered warehouse of its size that is free at its start (warehouses are numbered from 1 per size; one freed at minute t is free at t), opening the next number if none is free. Return (needed, assignment): needed maps each size that has at least one run to the number of warehouses opened, and assignment lists (task_id, start, warehouse_no) in (start, task_id) order. {{size_rule}} {{graph_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 6 000 tasks and about 150 000 runs; thousands of warehouses can be busy at once. every ≥ 1 and duration ≥ 1. Expected: O(R log R) for R runs. Scanning warehouses 1, 2, 3, … for a free one at every run is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Task names, sizes, periods and durations are hypothetical. The model ignores warehouse start-up time, auto-suspend and per-second billing, and gives each run a warehouse to itself; it measures the schedule's concurrency, not a recommendation to run one task per warehouse.
sections.criteria: Correct schedule expansion with the strict < horizon and the skip rule tied to the last run that ran; half-open intervals with freed warehouses reusable at the same minute; (start, task_id) order; lowest-numbered free warehouse via a heap of free numbers and a heap of busy ends; sizes as separate pools (Hard+); graph runs with children after all predecessors and the skip rule over the whole graph run (Very Hard); O(R log R); can prove the greedy is optimal and discuss resume costs and offset search.

clarifications.q: A run ends at minute 30 and another starts at 30. Can they share a warehouse?
clarifications.a: Yes. Intervals are half-open.

clarifications.q: Two runs of the same size start at the same minute. Which gets the lower number?
clarifications.a: The one with the smaller task_id, because runs are assigned in (start, task_id) order.

clarifications.q: Is the number of warehouses the peak number of overlapping runs?
clarifications.a: Yes, per size: assigning the lowest free warehouse in start order never opens more than the peak. The assignment must still follow the stated rule exactly.

clarifications.q: After a skipped run, when is the next attempt?
clarifications.a: At the next scheduled minute, first_start + (k + 1) × every; skipping does not shift the schedule.

clarifications.q: Are tasks given in any particular order?
clarifications.a: No.

hints: First expand every root's schedule into runs, applying the skip rule as you go (you only need the end of the last run that ran).
Sort the runs by (start, task_id). Keep, per size, a min-heap of (end, warehouse_no) for busy warehouses and a min-heap of free numbers.
Before assigning a run starting at t, move every busy warehouse with end ≤ t to the free heap; then pop the smallest free number, or open a new one.
(Graphs) Inside one graph run, a child's start is the maximum end of its predecessors: compute it in topological order.
followups: Prove that the lowest-free greedy in start order opens exactly the peak number of simultaneous runs, per size.
Warehouses take a minute to resume and are billed for at least a minute each time they resume. How does that change the objective, and would you still give every run its own warehouse?
The team may shift each task's first_start within its period. How would you search for offsets that lower the peak, and how good can a greedy be?
Some tasks could run on a larger shared warehouse instead. Sketch how you would decide which tasks to consolidate, and what you would measure to check the decision.

rules.ask: The specification assigns in order of start time. What goes wrong if you process runs by end time instead?
Thousands of warehouses are busy at once. What does finding the lowest free one cost per run, and which structure makes it O(log w)?
The sweep gives the count. How do you also produce the exact assignment, and why does the lowest free number matter?
A run takes 25 minutes and the period is 10. How many runs happen in an hour under the skip rule, and when does the next run start after a skip?
A child has two predecessors that finish at different times. When does it start, and how do you know its predecessors have been computed?

templates.title: Which staged files will the next bulk load pick up?
templates.subtopic: glob-to-regex translation, indexing history by key, retention-window boundaries

sections.scenario: A pipeline loads files that upstream systems drop into a cloud storage stage into warehouse tables with a bulk-load command. The load is idempotent because the platform remembers, for a limited time, which files it has already loaded into each table and skips them. Files whose history has been forgotten are a known trap: if a file is old and there is no remembered load for it, the loader cannot tell whether it was loaded, and by default it skips the file rather than risk a duplicate. Public bulk-loading documentation describes load metadata kept for 64 days; this exercise uses that number as its own rule (check current docs). The on-call engineer wants a dry run: for the files in the stage now, which would be loaded and which skipped, and why.
sections.problem: Implement select_files(files, history, patterns, now, load_uncertain). files lists (path, etag, last_modified); history lists load records (path, etag, loaded_at, status) for the target table; times are Unix seconds. A file is selected if its path matches at least one include pattern in full. Patterns are globs: * matches any run of characters except / (including none), ? exactly one character except /, and every other character matches itself (. is a literal dot). {{glob_rule}} A history record is remembered if now − loaded_at < 64 × 86 400; older records are forgotten. For each selected file: if a remembered record has the same path, the same etag and status LOADED, the file is SKIP_LOADED; otherwise, if any remembered record has the same path, it is LOAD (the file changed, so its status is known); otherwise, if now − last_modified ≥ 64 × 86 400 it is SKIP_UNCERTAIN, and if not, LOAD. Return [(path, status)] for the selected files, sorted by path. {{history_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 60 000 files and 60 000 history records per call, and a handful of patterns. Expected: O(F × P × L + H) for F files, P patterns of length L and H records. Scanning the history for every file is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Paths, etags, times and the 64-day window are hypothetical exercise values. Real bulk-load commands document their own pattern syntax (often a regular expression rather than a glob), options to force a reload or to load files whose status is unknown, and more detailed conditions for "unknown"; this exercise keeps one simplified rule. Paths in a call are unique.
sections.criteria: Correct glob semantics (* and ? never cross /, literal dots, full-path matches; **, exclusion and classes at Hard and Very Hard); the strict 64-day memory and the inclusive 64-day uncertainty boundary; same-path same-etag LOADED skipped, changed or failed files loaded (Very Hard); uncertain files skipped unless the switch is on; an index by path instead of a scan; patterns compiled once; sorted output; can discuss concurrent loads, in-place rewrites, listing cost and safe reloads.

clarifications.q: Does landing/*.csv.gz match landing/2026/a.csv.gz?
clarifications.a: No. * never crosses a /.

clarifications.q: A load record is exactly 64 days old. Is it remembered?
clarifications.a: No. Remembered means strictly less than 64 days old.

clarifications.q: A file was last modified exactly 64 days ago and was never loaded. Load or skip?
clarifications.a: Skip as uncertain. Uncertain starts at exactly 64 days.

clarifications.q: The same path was loaded twice with different etags. Which record matters?
clarifications.a: Any remembered LOADED record whose etag equals the file's current etag means the file is already loaded.

clarifications.q: Can I use fnmatch?
clarifications.a: Check its rules first: its * matches /, which this loader's does not.

hints: Translate each glob once into a regular expression (* → [^/]*, ? → [^/], other characters escaped) and use a full match.
Build a dict from path to the set of etags of remembered LOADED records, and remember separately which paths have any remembered record.
Then each file is a constant number of lookups plus the pattern matches.
followups: Two loads run concurrently against the same stage and table. What could go wrong with this dry run's answer, and how does a real loader avoid loading a file twice?
An upstream system rewrites files in place with new content but keeps the same name. What does the loader do, and what should the pipeline do instead?
The stage has 50 million files and the listing itself takes an hour. How would you restructure the paths and the patterns so each load lists only what it needs?
The team wants to reload a day of files after fixing a bug in the target table. Which options would you use, and how do you prevent duplicates in the table?

rules.ask: Does that library's * match /? Show a path where it gives a different answer from the loader's rule.
There are 60 000 files and 60 000 records. How many comparisons does your loop make, and what would you index by?
Is a record exactly 64 days old remembered in your code, and is a file exactly 64 days old uncertain? Point to the comparisons.
Why compare the etag and not only the path, and what does a matching path with a different etag tell you?
If you force the load, what happens to files that were already loaded, and how would you keep the table free of duplicates?

templates.title: Multi-cluster warehouse simulation — queueing, scale-out and scale-in, wait times and credits
templates.subtopic: discrete events, queues and heaps, billing rules

sections.scenario: A cloud data platform runs queries on virtual warehouses. A multi-cluster warehouse can add clusters of the same size when queries start to queue and shut them down when they sit idle, and each running cluster consumes credits by the second. The team that owns the warehouse {{warehouse}} wants to replay a day's query trace against a candidate scaling policy before changing it: how long did queries wait, how many clusters ran at the peak, and what would it cost? The policy below is this exercise's simplified version; real scaling policies differ, so check current docs.
sections.problem:
Implement simulate_warehouse(queries, policy). queries is a list of (query_id, arrival_s, duration_s) in arrival order; queries that arrive in the same second queue in list order. policy has slots (queries one cluster runs at once), min_clusters, max_clusters, startup_s, idle_s and credits_per_hour (per cluster). The warehouse resumes at the first arrival with min_clusters clusters, numbered from 1 and ready at once; each later cluster gets the next number. At every second t, apply these steps in order:

  1. Queries that finish at t (start + duration) free their slots. A cluster left with nothing running is idle from t.
  2. A cluster whose startup ends at t becomes ready, idle from t.
  3. Queries that arrive at t join the back of the queue.
  4. While the queue is not empty and a ready cluster has a free slot, the query at the head starts on the lowest-numbered ready cluster with a free slot. Its wait is t − arrival_s.
  5. Scale out. If the queue is still not empty, no cluster is starting, and there are fewer than max_clusters clusters (ready or starting), a new cluster starts; it becomes ready at t + startup_s.
  6. Scale in. Every ready cluster that has been idle for at least idle_s seconds shuts down at t, highest number first, as long as more than min_clusters clusters (ready or starting) remain.

The replay ends at the second the last query finishes, and every cluster still on stops then. Each cluster is billed from the second it started until it stopped, with a minimum of 60 seconds per cluster start. Return (max_wait, total_wait, peak_clusters, billed_seconds, credits): peak_clusters is the most clusters (ready or starting) at any second, billed_seconds is summed over clusters, and credits = billed_seconds × credits_per_hour / 3600 rounded to 3 decimal places. With no queries, return (0, 0, 0, 0, 0.0). {{size_rule}} {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 queries; a trace can span months, with quiet gaps of hours or days between bursts. All times are non-negative integers in seconds; duration_s ≥ 1, startup_s ≥ 1, idle_s ≥ 1, slots ≥ 1, 1 ≤ min_clusters ≤ max_clusters ≤ 10. Stepping through every second of the trace is far too slow; the intended solution is close to O(n log n + n · max_clusters).
sections.assumptions: The policy, sizes, credit rates and the trace are hypothetical. Every query takes the same time on any cluster and never fails. The warehouse does not suspend between the first arrival and the last finish. The 60-second minimum per cluster start and per-second billing are this exercise's rules; check current docs for the platform's billing.
sections.criteria: Correct replay of all six steps in order, including same-second finishes, arrivals and readiness; one starting cluster at a time; min_clusters and max_clusters counted with starting clusters; packing onto the lowest number; billing per cluster start with the 60-second minimum and the stop at the last finish; the empty trace; an event-driven loop that jumps between interesting seconds with a heap, not a second-by-second loop; a clear complexity argument; credible answers on load-dependent durations and cost attribution.

clarifications.q: Can a query start in the same second another finishes?
clarifications.a: Yes. Finishes free slots first (step 1), then arrivals queue (step 3), then dispatch runs (step 4).

clarifications.q: Why the lowest-numbered cluster, not the least loaded one?
clarifications.a: Packing work onto low numbers lets the high-numbered clusters go idle and shut down. It is part of the policy you are replaying.

clarifications.q: Can several clusters start at once when the queue is long?
clarifications.a: No. A new cluster starts only when no other cluster is starting, so a long queue adds one cluster per startup_s.

clarifications.q: Is a cluster that is still starting counted against max_clusters and min_clusters?
clarifications.a: Yes, in both. It is not ready, so it cannot run queries yet.

clarifications.q: A query arrives in exactly the second an idle cluster reaches idle_s. Does the cluster shut down?
clarifications.a: No. Dispatch (step 4) runs before scale-in (step 6), so the query starts on it and it is no longer idle.

clarifications.q: What if a cluster is still starting when the last query finishes?
clarifications.a: It stops then, and it is billed the 60-second minimum.

hints: Between two interesting seconds nothing changes. List the kinds of second that can change state: an arrival, a finish, a cluster becoming ready, and an idle cluster reaching idle_s.
Keep finishes in a min-heap of (finish_second, cluster). The next second to process is the smallest of the next arrival, the heap's top, the starting cluster's ready time and the idle deadlines.
An idle cluster's deadline only matters while there are more than min_clusters clusters. When can a cluster be idle while the queue is non-empty?
followups: Add a second policy that starts a cluster only when the queue is expected to keep it busy for several minutes. What would you need to estimate, and how would you compare the two policies on cost and on p95 wait?
Queries on a real warehouse slow down when more of them share a cluster. How would you change the model so that duration depends on the cluster's load, and what happens to your event loop?

Finance wants the cost of each query, not just the warehouse. How would you attribute the billed seconds, including the idle seconds and the 60-second minimums, to queries and to the teams that ran them?
The trace has 50 million queries across thousands of warehouses. How would you run the replay for every warehouse and every candidate policy, and what would you keep from each run?

rules.ask: The trace spans months. How many iterations is that, and which seconds can you skip without changing the answer?
What exactly is in your heap, and how do you make sure the idle deadlines and the starting cluster's ready time are not missed?
Your dispatch spreads queries across clusters. What does that do to scale-in and to the bill, compared with packing onto the lowest number?
Where does your billing first become a float, and would rounding each cluster's credits separately change the total?
The queue is first in, first out. What does sorting it each second cost when a burst leaves 5 000 queries waiting?

templates.title: Join ordering — the cheapest left-deep order by dynamic programming over subsets
templates.subtopic: subset DP, query optimisation, exact integer arithmetic

sections.scenario: A cloud data warehouse compiles every SQL query into a plan before a virtual warehouse runs it, and the order of the joins can change the work by orders of magnitude. The compiler estimates rows from table metadata. Analysts' dashboards join large fact tables to filtered dimensions, and you are asked to write the part of a simplified, teaching-sized compiler that picks the cheapest left-deep join order from given row estimates. The cost model here is this exercise's model, not any engine's.
sections.problem: Implement best_join_order(tables, predicates, allow_cross=True). tables maps each table name to its estimated rows after filters. predicates is a list of (a, b, d): a join predicate between tables a and b that keeps one of every d row pairs; several predicates on one pair multiply. The estimated rows of a set of tables S is rows(S) = floor(∏ rows of the tables in S / ∏ d of the predicates with both tables in S), computed exactly with integers. A left-deep order t1, t2, …, tn joins the result so far with one base table at a time; joining prefix P = {t1 … tk−1} with tk costs rows(P) + rows({tk}) + rows(P ∪ {tk}). The plan's cost is the sum over its joins; the first scan is free. Return (cost, order) for the cheapest order. If several orders cost the same, return the lexicographically smallest list of names. With allow_cross=False, every table after the first must share a predicate with a table already joined; if no order does, return None. With no tables, return (0, []); with one, (0, [name]). {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 16 tables and 40 predicates. Rows and d are positive integers; estimates can far exceed 2⁶³. Trying every order is n! (over 10¹³ for 16 tables); something close to O(2ⁿ · n) is expected, with the row estimate of each subset computed once.
sections.assumptions: Row estimates and selectivities are hypothetical; a real compiler also uses histograms, distinct counts, pruning statistics and run-time feedback. Only left-deep orders are considered here. Every predicate names two different tables in tables.
sections.criteria: A DP over subsets with each subset's estimate computed once and exactly; correct costs including the free first scan; the lexicographic tie rule; None only when cross products are forbidden and the graph is disconnected; the empty and single-table cases; integer arithmetic for estimates beyond 64 bits; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on bushy plans, estimate errors and very large joins.

clarifications.q: Is the cost symmetric in the first two tables?
clarifications.a: Yes, rows({a}) + rows({b}) + rows({a, b}) either way, which is why ties are common and the lexicographic rule matters.

clarifications.q: Do I round each join's estimate, or the final cost?
clarifications.a: Each rows(S) is rounded down on its own, from the exact product: multiply first, divide once. The cost is a sum of those integers.

clarifications.q: Does rows(S) depend on the order the tables were joined in?
clarifications.a: No. It depends only on the set, which is what makes a dynamic programme possible.

clarifications.q: What does lexicographically smallest mean for lists of names?
clarifications.a: Compare the first names; if equal, the second; and so on, using ordinary string comparison.

clarifications.q: With allow_cross=True, may I start with two tables that share no predicate?
clarifications.a: Yes. A cross product of two tiny filtered dimensions is sometimes the cheapest start.

hints: The cost of the next join depends only on the set already joined and the table added. Let best[P] be the cheapest cost to finish the plan when the tables in P are already joined.
Precompute rows(S) for every subset from a smaller subset: add one table, multiply its rows into the numerator and the d of its predicates into S into the denominator.
For the lexicographic rule, first compute best for every set, then rebuild the order from the front: at each step pick the smallest name that keeps the total optimal.
followups: Bushy plans can join two intermediate results. Extend the DP to bushy trees for this cost model. What is the new complexity?
The row estimate for one dimension was off by 1 000× because its filter is on a correlated column. How would you make the chosen plan robust to estimate errors?
Twenty-five tables appear in a generated query. What do you do when the exact DP is out of reach, and how do you bound how far from optimal you are?
The engine can change join order at run time when it sees actual row counts. What would you measure during execution, and when is it worth re-planning?

rules.ask: Build a three-table query where joining the smallest result next is not optimal. What does your greedy miss?
How many orders are there for 16 tables, and how long would costing each one take?
The estimates exceed 2⁶³. Where could floating point change your answer, and how do you keep it exact?
What is the key of your memo, how many states does it hold, and is the recursion depth a concern?
For this cost model, is a bushy plan ever cheaper than every left-deep one? Give an example or an argument.

templates.title: Debug a semi-structured JSON flattener — nested arrays, nulls, key collisions and paths
templates.subtopic: recursive flattening, paths, nulls, depth limits

sections.scenario: Raw {{source}} events land in a cloud warehouse as JSON documents in a semi-structured column. A helper flattens each document into one row of path → value pairs, and those pairs feed a column-discovery job and a data-quality check. Several complaints arrive. A data-quality rule says that no orders ever have a null coupon, which is not true. Customers with no tags vanish from a count of customers by number of tags. Two fields, id and ID, are reported as one. A field named ip address is reported as if it were nested. With a depth limit set, one level too many is expanded. The helper below is the suspect. Its path syntax is this exercise's, close to but not the same as the platform's own path notation.
sections.problem:
Fix flatten_records(records, max_depth=None) so that it meets this specification. records is a list of JSON objects (Python dicts); return one dict per record, in order. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Paths. A top-level key k has path k. A key k inside an object at path p has path p.k. An array element at index i has path p[i]. Indexes start at 0.
  2. Quoting. A key that is not a plain identifier (letters A–Z or a–z, digits and _, not starting with a digit) is written as ["k"] instead, with no dot before it, and any \ or " inside it is escaped with a backslash: geo["ip address"], ["x-ray"].on. Keys are case-sensitive: id and ID are different paths.
  3. Leaves. Strings, numbers, booleans and JSON nulls (None) are leaves: the row maps the path to the value, and a null is kept. An empty object or empty array is also a leaf, kept as {} or [].
  4. Depth. A value's depth is the number of path segments to it, so a top-level value has depth 1. When max_depth is set, an object or array at depth max_depth is not expanded: it is a leaf, kept whole. With None, there is no limit.
  5. Records. The record itself is never a leaf: an empty record gives an empty row {}.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Up to 15 000 documents and a million leaves, processed in linear time. Keys can be any string.
sections.assumptions: Documents and field names are hypothetical. Every record is a dict; JSON has already been parsed. Duplicate keys inside one JSON object were resolved by the parser before this step.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; nulls kept; empty objects and arrays kept as values while an empty record stays an empty row; case-sensitive keys; complete quoting with escapes; the depth boundary at exactly max_depth; minimal, linear fixes; a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Should a null field appear in the row?
clarifications.a: Yes, as None. A null field and a missing field mean different things to the data-quality check.

clarifications.q: Why keep {} and []?
clarifications.a: So that "has no tags" stays visible. A row without the path cannot be told apart from a document that never had the field.

clarifications.q: Is user_id an identifier? Is 2fa? Is café?
clarifications.a: user_id is. 2fa starts with a digit, so it is quoted. café has a letter outside A–Z, so it is quoted too.

clarifications.q: With max_depth=2, what happens to {"a": {"b": {"c": 1}}}?
clarifications.a: a is at depth 1 and is expanded; a.b is at depth 2, so it is kept whole: {"a.b": {"c": 1}}.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Flatten {"coupon": null, "tags": []} by hand, then run it through the code.
Read the comment next to the line that changes keys. Is it true of JSON keys?
Write down the depth of a, a.b and a.b.c, then read the condition that decides whether to expand.
List keys that need quoting: a dot, a space, a hyphen, a leading digit, a quote. Which of them does _segment catch?
followups: A column-discovery job turns paths into typed columns. One document has price as a number and another as a string. What should the column's type be, and what happens to the values that do not fit?
Arrays of line items make one row per record very wide. When would you flatten an array into one row per element instead, and what keys do you carry onto each row?
A producer renames userId to user_id mid-month. How would you detect it from the flattened output, and what would you tell the consumers?
The flattener runs inside the warehouse's ingestion, on billions of documents a day. What would you push into SQL (a flatten function over the semi-structured column) and what would you keep in code?

rules.ask: Two fields, id and ID, are both present. What does your version return, and who decides whether they are the same field?
str.isidentifier() accepts café and other non-ASCII letters. Does that match the specification, and what would you use instead?
A malicious document is nested 5 000 levels deep. What happens to your recursion, and how would you avoid it?
Why would turning a nested value into a string be a problem for the column-discovery job that reads these rows?
Which values does that condition drop, and which of them should be kept?

templates.title: Bulk loading from cloud storage with load history and deduplication
templates.subtopic: file ingestion, load metadata, idempotency, deduplication

redelivery: the same file name with corrected contents
a full re-send of the last 30 days under new file names

sections.scenario: A cloud data platform loads files from cloud object storage into tables. Each table remembers which files it has already loaded for a limited time, so a repeated load skips them; in this exercise that load history is kept for {{history_days}} days (this exercise's rule; check current docs for the platform's actual retention, which differs between bulk and continuous loading). A retail data team receives about {{daily_files}} files a day, sized {{file_size}}, from {{partners}} partners who drop sales, inventory and returns files into one bucket. Partners sometimes re-send data as {{redelivery}}. The team needs every row loaded once, nothing lost, and an answer to "was this file loaded, when, and with how many rows?"
sections.problem: Design the ingestion from the bucket to the warehouse tables. Cover how new files are discovered (listing versus event notifications), how loads are batched and sized, what makes a retried or repeated load harmless at the file level and at the row level, what happens once a file is older than the load history, how corrected re-sends and full re-sends are handled, schema drift and bad rows, your own audit table of loads, and the metrics and alerts that show the pipeline is healthy.
sections.constraints: A partner's late or corrected file must replace the rows it corrects, never add to them. A load can fail half-way and be retried. Event notifications can be delayed, duplicated or lost. Some files arrive weeks late. The warehouse is billed by compute time, so loading many tiny files one at a time is expensive.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, partner counts, retention periods and formats are hypothetical. Files are CSV or JSON with a header or a schema per partner. Each row carries the partner's own business key (for example store, SKU and business date) and the partner's extract time.
sections.criteria: Clear split between file-level and row-level idempotency; a durable manifest beyond the platform's load history; a landing table with file lineage and a merge by business key with a deterministic tie rule; a stated policy for files older than the history; corrected and full re-sends replacing rows, never adding; listing reconciliation behind notifications; schema drift and bad rows isolated per partner; batching sized for compute cost; health metrics (files discovered versus loaded, lag, rejected rows, duplicates suppressed); a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: How does the platform decide a file was already loaded?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, by its path and a checksum of its contents, for as long as the load history lasts. A changed file under the same name is treated as new.

clarifications.q: What happens to a file older than the history?
clarifications.a: The platform can no longer tell whether it was loaded. In this exercise it skips it by default and can be told to load it anyway. Decide what your pipeline does.

clarifications.q: Are rows unique across files?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. A re-send repeats rows, and a correction changes some of them. Rows are unique per partner business key and extract time.

clarifications.q: Who needs the audit?
clarifications.a: Partner support ("did you get our file?") and finance, who reconcile partner totals monthly.

hints: Separate "was this file loaded" (file level) from "is this row already in the table" (row level). The load history only answers the first, and only for a while.
Keep your own manifest of files and their outcomes, keyed by path and checksum, with no expiry.
Load raw files into a landing table with the file name and row number, then merge into the modelled table by business key, keeping the latest extract.
followups: A partner re-sends {{redelivery}}. Walk through what each layer does, and how you prove no row was double counted.
Event notifications were lost for six hours. How do you find the missing files, and how do you know you found all of them?
One partner adds a column and changes a date format on the same day. What happens to that day's loads, and what do the other partners see?
Finance asks for the load history of a file from 200 days ago. Where does that answer come from?
At {{daily_files}} files a day, most under a megabyte, compute cost doubles. What do you change in batching and file sizes?

rules.ask: Forcing a reload skips the platform's duplicate check. What stops that from loading a file twice into the final table?
A partner sends a corrected file under the same name. Does your design load it, and what happens to the rows it corrected?
What is your merge key, and what happens when two files in one batch carry the same key with different extract times?
Notifications can be lost. What runs alongside them so that a lost notification is noticed?
Which part of your design gives exactly-once at the row level: the platform's load history, your manifest, or the merge? Why?

incidents: Load history is kept for {{history_days}} days in this exercise. A partner re-uploads a file from {{history_days}} days and one hour ago under its original name and unchanged contents.
A partner's export job is fixed and re-sends {{redelivery}}. That morning the sales table's revenue for the period rises by 9%.
Event notifications from the bucket stop for six hours during a cloud-provider incident. Dashboards show no errors, only lower row counts.

templates.title: Zero-downtime migration from a legacy warehouse — dual running and reconciliation
templates.subtopic: migration, parallel runs, reconciliation, cutover and rollback

legacy: a Hadoop cluster with Hive tables
deadline: 9 months, when the hardware support contract ends
6 months, before the data centre closes

sections.scenario: A company runs its reporting on {{legacy}} with about {{tables}} tables and {{data_size}} of data, feeding {{consumers}}. It is moving to a cloud data platform, and the hardware must be gone in {{deadline}}. Leadership's condition is that no report is wrong and no consumer is down on the day it moves. Nightly loads keep changing the data during the whole migration, and the two systems' SQL dialects differ in data types, NULL and empty-string handling, time zones, rounding and case sensitivity.
sections.problem: Design the migration. Cover the inventory and the order in which tables, pipelines and consumers move; the initial copy and how the cloud copy keeps up while the legacy system is still the source of truth; how SQL and pipelines are translated and tested; dual running and the reconciliation that proves the two systems agree (what you compare, at what grain, with which tolerances); how each consumer is cut over and rolled back; when the legacy system is finally switched off; and how you report progress to leadership.
sections.constraints: No consumer may be offline during its cutover. The legacy system has little spare capacity, so extraction and reconciliation queries cannot run at peak hours. Some tables are updated in place by nightly jobs. The budget allows both systems to run in parallel for a limited time only. Some consumers are owned by other teams.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, counts, deadlines and system types are hypothetical. Network transfer and storage costs are known. Both systems can export data to object storage. The cloud platform's SQL dialect is documented, and an automated translator handles most but not all of the SQL.
sections.criteria: An inventory with lineage and a domain-by-domain plan; an initial copy plus incremental catch-up while legacy remains the source of truth; tested translation with known dialect traps (types, NULLs, time zones, rounding, case); multi-grain reconciliation with classified, explained differences; reversible per-consumer cutovers; a clear rule for switching off and archiving; cost of parallel running managed; honest, measurable progress reporting; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Do we move everything at once?
clarifications.a: That is your decision. Leadership wants to know the risk of each option.

clarifications.q: Are differences ever acceptable?
clarifications.a: Only explained ones, such as a documented rounding or time-zone rule. Every difference must be classified.

clarifications.q: Who owns the consumers?
clarifications.a: Analytics owns most dashboards. Finance owns the extracts, and three product teams own applications that read tables directly.

clarifications.q: Can consumers switch back after cutover?
clarifications.a: They must be able to, until the legacy system is turned off.

hints: Migrate by consumer-facing domain with its whole lineage (sources, pipelines, tables and consumers), not table by table at random.
Reconcile at several grains: row counts, aggregates by partition and key columns, then row-level hashes where aggregates disagree.
Make a cutover a configuration change (a connection or a view) that can be reversed in minutes.
followups: Reconciliation shows a 0.02% revenue difference on one table. Walk through how you find whether it is translation, data movement or a legacy bug.
A nightly job updates rows in place on the legacy side during your copy. How do you keep the cloud copy consistent?
Halfway through, the deadline moves three months earlier. What do you change, and what do you refuse to change?
How do you know it is safe to switch off the legacy system, and what do you archive first?
How would you show leadership, every week, that the migration is on track, with numbers rather than status colours?

rules.ask: What happens on the morning after a big-bang cutover when 3% of the dashboards are wrong, and how do you roll back only those?
Row counts match but revenue does not. What else do you compare, and at what grain?
The two systems format decimals, timestamps and NULLs differently. How do you make a row hash comparable across them?
If a pipeline writes to both systems and one write fails, which one is right, and how do you repair the other?
The translator converts 92% of the SQL. How do you find the queries that translate without errors but give different answers?

incidents: Two weeks after a domain cuts over, finance finds that month-end revenue in the cloud system differs from the legacy figure by 0.02%, and the legacy system is the one that was wrong.
A reconciliation query on {{legacy}} runs at 9 a.m. by mistake and slows the morning reports that are still served from it.
Ten days before the deadline, 4% of the consumers have not cut over because their owners have not tested them, and the legacy system cannot be kept on.

templates.title: One analytics product, many tenants — schema per tenant or shared tables with row access policies
templates.subtopic: multi-tenant isolation, row access policies, per-tenant schemas, cost attribution

custom_fields: up to 20 custom fields per tenant
up to 200 custom fields per tenant
regions: two regions, with EU tenants' data kept in the EU

sections.scenario: A SaaS company sells a customer-support product and builds its in-product analytics on a cloud data platform. It has {{tenants}} tenant companies; the largest tenant holds about {{largest_share}} of all rows, while most tenants are tiny. Each tenant's users see dashboards of tickets, agents, response times and satisfaction, and some tenants add their own fields ({{custom_fields}}). Large tenants also want a direct, governed way to query their own data, and the company runs in {{regions}}. The data team must choose between a schema (or database) per tenant and shared tables where every row carries a tenant id and access is filtered by a row access policy, and it must be able to say what each tenant costs to serve.
sections.problem: Design the data model and the isolation scheme. Cover: the core tables (tickets, ticket events, agents, satisfaction surveys) and their keys; where the tenant id lives and how it is enforced on every read path (dashboards through a service account, direct tenant queries, internal analysts); how custom fields are stored and queried; the trade-offs of schema-per-tenant versus shared tables versus a hybrid (dedicated objects for the largest tenants), including deployment of schema changes, onboarding and offboarding, clustering and pruning for tiny and huge tenants, and the cost of many small objects; and how compute and storage cost is attributed to tenants.
sections.constraints: A tenant must never see another tenant's rows, through any path, including cached results and exports. A tenant's data can be deleted completely on request within a stated time. Schema changes ship to every tenant on one release cadence. Data residency, where it applies, is never broken by replication or by internal analysts' queries.
sections.assumptions: Tenant counts, shares and limits are hypothetical. Row access policies, secure views, role-based access and per-tenant databases are features of the platform in this exercise; check current docs for their exact behaviour and limits. Internal analysts may query across tenants only in aggregated, approved views.
sections.criteria: Tenant id on every row and enforced by policy on every read path, not by caller discipline; a clear, justified choice (or hybrid with a promotion rule) weighing deployment, deletion, residency, pruning and object count; custom fields modelled for filtering and typing; deletion including recovery copies; cost attribution per tenant from query history; separate compute for heavy tenants; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do tenants query the warehouse directly?
clarifications.a: The largest ones want to, through their own login or through data shared to their own account. Everyone else uses the dashboards.

clarifications.q: How are dashboards authenticated?
clarifications.a: Through a backend service account that runs queries on behalf of a signed-in tenant user. You decide how the tenant context reaches the query.

clarifications.q: Can tenants define arbitrary custom fields?
clarifications.a: Yes, typed (text, number, date, picklist), within the stated limit, and they can rename or retire them.

clarifications.q: What does offboarding require?
clarifications.a: All of the tenant's data removed from the platform within 30 days of the request, with evidence; you say what happens to backups and recovery copies.

clarifications.q: Do internal teams need cross-tenant data?
clarifications.a: Yes, for benchmarks such as "median first response time across tenants", only in aggregate and above a minimum group size.

hints: Start from the threat model: list every read path and say where the tenant filter is applied on each. A filter the caller can forget is not isolation.
Shared tables make schema changes and small tenants cheap; dedicated objects make deletion, residency and very large tenants simpler. A hybrid needs a rule for when a tenant moves.
Custom fields can be a typed key-value table, a semi-structured column, or generated columns per tenant. Think about how a dashboard filters and groups on them.
followups: Write the row access policy logic (in pseudocode) for shared tables, including how the dashboard service passes the tenant context and how an internal analyst role is handled.
The largest tenant holds {{largest_share}} of rows. How do clustering and pruning behave for it and for a tenant with 2,000 tickets in the same table?
A tenant asks to be deleted. Walk through shared tables versus a dedicated schema, including time travel and recovery copies.
A schema change adds a column to tickets. How does it reach {{tenants}} tenants in each design, and how do you test it?
Show how one month's compute cost is split across tenants when dashboards for many tenants share one warehouse.

rules.ask: You will have {{tenants}} schemas. How do you deploy one column change to all of them, and what do you do when it fails halfway?
The dashboard service connects with one service account. How does the policy know which tenant is asking, and what stops the service from passing the wrong one?
Why a secure view rather than an ordinary view here, and what does that cost the optimiser?
A tenant filters a dashboard on a custom date field stored inside a semi-structured column. How fast is that, and how do you validate the type?
A dashboard groups by three custom fields. How many self-joins is that, and how would you avoid them?

incidents: A dashboard query's cached result was served to a user of another tenant because the cache key did not include the tenant context passed by the service account; with {{tenants}} tenants the blast radius is unknown until the query log is checked.
An onboarding script creates a schema per new tenant; a failed release left some schemas one column behind, and every dashboard query for those tenants errors after the next deploy.
The largest tenant, with {{largest_share}} of rows, runs heavy direct queries on the shared dashboard warehouse at month end, and every small tenant's dashboards time out.

templates.title: Device events as semi-structured data — what to flatten, how to survive drift
templates.subtopic: semi-structured columns, flattening, schema drift, pruning and query performance

drift: a few new fields a month
new fields every week, and some fields change type

sections.scenario: A connected-fitness company streams JSON events from its app and devices into a cloud data platform: about {{daily_events}} events a day across {{event_types}} event types. A typical event has an envelope (event id, type, device id, user id, app version, timestamps) and a payload whose shape depends on the type: workout summaries, heart-rate samples as arrays, nested settings objects, and error reports. {{app_versions}} app versions are live at once, and the payload drifts: {{drift}}. Today everything lands as one semi-structured column, and analysts write path expressions against it; their queries are slow and sometimes silently wrong after a release.
sections.problem: Design the model from landing to analysis. Cover: the raw landing table (what is typed, what stays semi-structured, and the keys and load metadata kept); which fields are extracted into typed columns and which tables are flattened (for example, one row per heart-rate sample or per workout lap); how schema drift is detected and handled (new fields, renamed fields, type changes, JSON null versus missing) without losing data or breaking queries; how queries prune by time and device; and the contract between app teams and the data team for event payloads.
sections.constraints: No event is dropped because its payload is unexpected; unparseable or invalid records are kept and counted. A field's meaning never changes under the same name in a typed table. Analysts can query new fields within a day of a release without a code change from the data team, but dashboards read only typed, documented columns. Raw events are kept for a stated period for replay.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, type counts and drift rates are hypothetical. In this exercise the platform stores a semi-structured column in a columnar form and can prune on some paths, but values whose type varies across rows, dates stored as strings and arrays get less benefit; check current docs for the exact behaviour. Timestamps in payloads are device clocks and can be wrong.
sections.criteria: Typed envelope and kept raw payload with load metadata; a principled rule for which paths become typed columns and which arrays become child tables at their own grain; drift detected per app version with rejects kept and counted, never silent NULLs; null versus missing preserved; pruning on typed time and device columns; a contract with versioning that tolerates old clients; storage and row estimates; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do all event types need typed tables?
clarifications.a: No. About a dozen types serve most dashboards; the long tail is explored ad hoc.

clarifications.q: What does a type change look like?
clarifications.a: For example, distance changed from a number in metres to a string such as "5.2 km" in one app version.

clarifications.q: Are arrays large?
clarifications.a: Heart-rate samples can have thousands of elements per workout; most other arrays are small.

clarifications.q: Is a JSON null the same as a missing field?
clarifications.a: Not to the app teams: null means "measured, no value", missing means "this version does not send it". You decide how the model keeps the difference.

clarifications.q: Can the app teams change the payload format?
clarifications.a: They can add versioned schemas and follow a contract you propose, but old app versions stay in the field for months.

hints: Keep the raw envelope typed and the payload semi-structured; extract the paths that are filtered, joined or aggregated often into typed columns, with the extraction rule versioned.
Arrays that analysts aggregate (samples, laps) deserve their own flattened table at their own grain, keyed by event id and index.
Drift is a data-quality signal: profile new paths and type mismatches per app version each load, and route bad values to a rejects column or table instead of casting them to NULL.
followups: Estimate rows in a flattened heart-rate sample table at {{daily_events}} events a day if 2% of events are workouts with 1,800 samples each. Partitioning, clustering and retention?
distance changes from a number to a string in one app version. What happens to the typed column, the dashboards and the history?
An analyst wants a new field from yesterday's release. What do they query today, and how does it become a typed column?
Write the check that would have caught a release where user_id moved from the envelope into the payload.
Compare three ways to keep {{event_types}} event types: one wide table, one table per type, or a typed envelope plus a semi-structured payload with a few flattened children. When does each win?

rules.ask: Flattening a workout with 1,800 samples multiplies rows. Which queries need the flattened table, and which should stay on the summary?
With {{event_types}} types and new ones each month, who creates the tables, and how does a cross-type query (all events for one device in an hour) work?
An analyst filters on a payload path for one day. How much of the table does that read, and what would make it prune?
A cast fails for one app version. Does the row disappear, become NULL, or go somewhere you can count?
Old app versions stay in the field for months and ignore the new contract. What does your pipeline do with their events?

incidents: An app release sends distance as a string; the typed column casts it to NULL, and weekly distance on dashboards drops by a fifth for users on that version without any load error.

A query over one day of workouts scans the whole landing table: the analysts' filter is a payload timestamp stored as a string, not the typed event date the table is clustered on; at {{daily_events}} events a day the warehouse runs for hours.

With {{drift}}, a renamed field appears under its new name in new app versions while old versions keep the old name; one dashboard counts only the new name and reports a false 40% drop in a feature's use.

templates.title: A retail star schema — returns, promotions, currencies and stores that arrive late
templates.subtopic: dimensional design, conformed dimensions, late-arriving dimension members, currency conversion

sections.scenario: A retail chain, a customer of a cloud data platform, sells through {{stores}} stores and an online channel in {{currencies}} currencies, about {{daily_lines}} sales lines a day. Returns can happen in any store, weeks later, with or without the original receipt. Promotions (percentage off, buy-one-get-one, basket thresholds, loyalty coupons) can stack, and a line can carry several. New stores, pop-ups and franchise stores start trading before the master-data team registers them: their sales arrive with a store code the warehouse has never seen, and the store's details follow up to {{store_lag_days}} days later. Finance reports in one group currency; country managers report in local currency.
sections.problem: Design the star schema. Cover: the grain of the sales fact and of a returns fact (or one fact with signed rows), with their keys and measures; the dimensions (date, store, product, customer or loyalty member, promotion, currency) and which are slowly changing and how; how multiple promotions per line are represented (a bridge, an allocation, or a factless coverage fact); how returns link to the original sale when they can and what happens when they cannot; how currency conversion is modelled (which rate, which date, stored or computed); and how a sale with an unknown store code is loaded and later corrected.
sections.constraints: Sales are never dropped or delayed because a dimension member is missing. Reported net sales for a closed month change only through a documented restatement. Amounts are stored in the transaction currency, in minor units, with conversion reproducible. A store that moves region keeps its history in the region it belonged to when it sold.
sections.assumptions: Store counts, volumes, currency counts and lags are hypothetical. Exchange rates come from a daily reference feed. Product and store master data is owned by other teams. Discounts are known at line level from the point-of-sale system.
sections.criteria: Explicit grains for sales and returns with signed or separate facts; conformed date, store, product, promotion and currency dimensions with justified SCD choices and both "as was" and "as is" reporting; promotions modelled without double-counting (bridge with allocation or per-promotion discount rows); returns linked when possible and handled when not; amounts in transaction currency with reproducible conversion; inferred members for late stores, corrected without losing sales; clustering for the dominant filters; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do returns carry the original receipt?
clarifications.a: Most do. About a fifth are returns without a receipt, refunded at the current price.

clarifications.q: How does finance convert currency?
clarifications.a: At the daily reference rate of the transaction date. Country managers use local currency only. You decide what to store.

clarifications.q: Can a line have several promotions?
clarifications.a: Yes, up to four; the point-of-sale system records each promotion's discount on the line.

clarifications.q: When a store changes region, how should last year's sales be reported?
clarifications.a: Both ways: "as it was" for financial history and "as it is now" for like-for-like comparisons. Say which is the default.

clarifications.q: What do we know about an unknown store code on arrival?
clarifications.a: Only the code and the currency of its sales.

hints: State the grain of each fact in one sentence before naming columns; a sales line and a return line are different events.
A late-arriving store can be loaded as an inferred (placeholder) dimension row keyed by its code, updated in place when the master data arrives; history starts from there.
Store amounts in transaction currency and convert in a view or a derived column using a rate table keyed by currency and date, so a rate correction does not require reloading facts.
followups: Write the definition of net sales in group currency for a month, including returns of sales from earlier months and returns without a receipt.
A line carries a 20% discount and a basket coupon. How do your promotion tables answer "sales lift and discount cost by promotion" without double-counting?
A store's code arrives {{store_lag_days}} days before its master data. What do the dashboards show in between, and what changes when the master data lands?
The rate feed corrects last Tuesday's rate for one currency. What changes in the warehouse and in reports?
At {{daily_lines}} lines a day, how do you cluster or partition the facts, and what do most queries filter on?

rules.ask: The store changed region in March. Show the two queries for "as it was" and "as it is now" against your store dimension.
A line with two promotions appears twice in the bridge. How does a SUM of sales over promotions avoid counting the line twice?
You mapped the unknown store to one default member. When the real store arrives, how do last week's sales move to it?
The rate for last Tuesday was corrected. Which rows do you rewrite, and how do you prove the restated total?
How does a return of last month's sale show in this month's net sales and in last month's return rate?

incidents: A new store traded for {{store_lag_days}} days before registration; its sales were mapped to a single "unknown" member and, when the store arrived, they stayed there, so the region's like-for-like growth was understated for the quarter.
A promotion bridge without an allocation factor made total discount cost by promotion exceed total discount on the receipts by 18% for basket-threshold offers.

The reference rate for one of {{currencies}} currencies was loaded a day late; facts converted at load time used the previous day's rate and the month's group-currency sales were restated after close.

templates.title: A query-history model for workload analysis — queued, compiling and executing time
templates.subtopic: query history facts, warehouse dimensions with size history, time breakdowns, query fingerprints

sections.scenario: A platform team inside a large company runs {{warehouses}} virtual warehouses on a cloud data platform for dozens of teams, about {{daily_queries}} queries a day from dashboards, scheduled pipelines and people. The platform exposes query history (text, user, role, warehouse, start and end times, bytes scanned, partitions scanned and total, and a breakdown of time spent compiling, queued and executing) and warehouse metering, with a delay of up to {{history_latency}} in this exercise. The team wants its own model of this history, kept for {{retention_days}} days and longer in aggregate, to answer: which workloads queue and on which warehouses, whether a warehouse should be resized or given more clusters, which repeated queries cost the most, and what each team spends.
sections.problem: Design the workload-analysis model. Cover: the query fact (grain, keys, the time breakdown as separate measures, and status); dimensions for warehouse (with size and cluster settings as history), user, role, team and workload (from query tags or a mapping); a query fingerprint (the query text with literals replaced) as a dimension; how incremental loads handle the history's delay and late updates for long-running queries; how compute credits, which are metered per warehouse rather than per query, are allocated to queries and teams; and the aggregates that serve "queued time by warehouse and hour", "top fingerprints by cost" and "spend by team".
sections.constraints: Every query is counted once, even when it appears in the history before it finishes and again after. A warehouse's size at the time of a query is reproducible after it is resized. Allocated credits for a warehouse-hour sum exactly to its metered credits. Query text can contain literals with customer data and must be access-controlled; the fingerprint is not.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, warehouse counts, latencies and retention are hypothetical; check current docs for the platform's actual query history columns, retention and delay. Teams tag their queries inconsistently; a mapping from user or role to team exists for the rest.
sections.criteria: Query grain with a MERGE on query id over a delay-aware window; the time breakdown as separate measures, including the two kinds of queueing; warehouse settings as history joined by time; fingerprints defined with their limits; credits allocated so that each warehouse-hour reconciles to metering, idle time explicit; text access-controlled; retention and aggregates sized; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is queued time one number?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the history separates time queued while the warehouse was starting (provisioning) from time queued because the warehouse was busy (overload). Keep them apart.

clarifications.q: Can a query appear before it finishes?
clarifications.a: Yes. A running query can appear with a partial record and is updated when it ends.

clarifications.q: How are credits allocated to queries?
clarifications.a: You choose. Execution time weighted by warehouse size within each warehouse-hour is common; say what you do with idle time.

clarifications.q: Do teams tag queries?
clarifications.a: Pipelines usually do; dashboards and people rarely do.

clarifications.q: Should failed and cancelled queries count?
clarifications.a: Yes, they used compute. Keep their status and error class.

hints: Grain: one row per query id, with start time, end time and each time component as its own measure. Load it as a MERGE on query id over a window wider than the history's delay.
Warehouse settings are a type 2 dimension (size, min and max clusters, scaling policy) from a settings-change log or periodic snapshots; join by time, not by current value.
Allocate each warehouse-hour's metered credits over the queries that ran in it, then carry idle credit as its own line so the totals reconcile.
followups: Define "queued share" for a warehouse-hour precisely. When does it argue for a bigger warehouse and when for more clusters?
Write the allocation rule for a warehouse-hour in which three queries ran for 10, 20 and 30 minutes and the warehouse was idle for 20 minutes.
How do you compute a fingerprint so that WHERE id = 5 and WHERE id = 7 match, but two different reports do not? What can go wrong?
The history arrives up to {{history_latency}} late and long queries are updated after they end. Design the incremental load and its watermark.
At {{daily_queries}} queries a day, kept {{retention_days}} days at full grain: storage, clustering, and what you aggregate for longer.

rules.ask: A dashboard query waited four minutes in the queue and ran for two seconds. Which number does your model blame, and what does the team see?
Query text contains customer literals. Who can read it in your model, and what can everyone else group by?
A warehouse ran one query a minute all day and was idle in between. Does the idle credit vanish, go to the queries, or get its own line?
The warehouse was resized yesterday. How do last week's queries know the size they ran on?
A long query appears first as running and again when it finishes. How do you avoid counting it twice?

incidents: The incremental load used a watermark equal to the last loaded end time; with history arriving up to {{history_latency}} late, a day of queries from {{warehouses}} warehouses was skipped, and team spend for that week was under-reported by 6%.
A warehouse's size was read from the current settings; after it was halved, last quarter's cost per fingerprint was recomputed at the new size and two teams' chargebacks changed after invoicing.
Queued time was reported as a single number; a warehouse with long provisioning queues (cold starts after auto-suspend) was given more clusters, which did not help and doubled its peak spend.
