templates.title: Warehouse credits per hour — per-second billing and a 60-second minimum after each resume
templates.subtopic: event log to runs, state changes, interval splitting at hour boundaries, minimum charges

sections.scenario: A company runs several virtual warehouses on a cloud data platform (here {{warehouse_list}}). A warehouse uses compute credits only while it runs: auto-resume starts it when a query arrives and auto-suspend stops it after a quiet spell, so it can start and stop many times an hour. In this exercise (check current docs for the actual rules) a running warehouse is billed per second at its size's credits_per_hour from warehouse_sizes, and each time it resumes it is billed for at least 60 seconds. The FinOps team wants credits per warehouse and hour, computed from the warehouse event log, to check against the platform's metering and to find warehouses that pay mostly for minimums.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns warehouse_name, hour_start, billed_seconds, credits: one row per warehouse and UTC hour that has at least one billed second before report_end, here {{report_end}}, ordered by warehouse_name, hour_start. {{events_rule}} A run starts when a suspended warehouse resumes and ends at its next SUSPEND (or at report_end, if it is still running then). It is billed for every second it runs, and if it ran for less than 60 seconds it is billed as though it kept running, at its last size, until 60 seconds after its resume. Each resume pays its own minimum, so the minimums of two runs a few seconds apart can overlap, and both are billed. Billed time is split at hour boundaries: billed_seconds is the number of billed seconds in the hour, summed over runs, and credits is Σ(seconds × credits_per_hour) / 3600 over those seconds, rounded to 4 decimal places once, at the end. Nothing at or after report_end is billed. {{end_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). An hour is [hh:00:00, hh+1:00:00) in UTC; a run that suspends exactly at hh:00:00 bills nothing in the hour that starts then. No two events of one warehouse share a timestamp. The sample has {{events}} events; production has thousands of warehouses and millions of events a day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical warehouses, times and quantities. The rate table (X-Small 1, Small 2, Medium 4, Large 8, X-Large 16 credits per hour) and the billing rule are this exercise's; check current docs. In this exercise a resize changes the rate at that instant and does not start a new minimum. Multi-cluster warehouses, serverless features and cloud-services credits are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Runs built from the event log with LAG/LEAD and, at the hardest level, no-op events removed by state change; the 60-second minimum applied per resume, as running time after the run, at the run's last size; size intervals intersected with runs; intervals split at hour boundaries with exact boundary handling; report_end respected, with open runs billed up to it; exact integer sums before one rounding; deterministic ordering; can explain metering differences, padding waste and incremental state.

clarifications.q: A warehouse runs for 20 seconds. How much is billed?
clarifications.a: 60 seconds at its size: the run is billed as though it ran until 60 seconds after its resume.

clarifications.q: It resumes at 10:59:50 and suspends at 10:59:55. Which hours get the seconds?
clarifications.a: 10 seconds in the 10:00 row and 50 seconds in the 11:00 row; the minimum is billed as running time, so it follows on after the run.

clarifications.q: It resumes at 10:00:00, suspends at 10:00:20, resumes at 10:00:30 and suspends at 10:00:40. How many seconds?
clarifications.a: 120. Each resume pays its own 60-second minimum: [10:00:00, 10:01:00) and [10:00:30, 10:01:30), even though they overlap.

clarifications.q: Should hours with no billed seconds appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only hours with at least one billed second.

clarifications.q: Should I round credits per run?
clarifications.a: No. Sum the exact credits for the hour, then round once to 4 decimal places.

hints: Turn the log into runs first: order each warehouse's RESUME and SUSPEND events and pair each RESUME with the event after it (LAG and LEAD over the warehouse's events). If the log can hold no-ops, keep only events whose type differs from the previous RESUME or SUSPEND.

A run's billed end is the later of its end and resume + 60 seconds, and never later than report_end. If sizes change, build size intervals (each RESIZE until the next) and intersect them with the run.

To split an interval at hours, generate the hours it touches with generate_series(date_trunc('hour', start), end - INTERVAL '1 microsecond', INTERVAL '1 hour') and take the overlap with each. Sum seconds × rate as integers before dividing by 3600.
followups: Your totals differ from the platform's metering by a few percent. List the causes you would check first, in order.
Write the query that finds warehouses where the minimum's padding is more than 20% of billed credits, and say what you would recommend to their owners.
Multi-cluster warehouses bill each cluster separately, with its own start. How does the model and this query change?
At millions of events a day, make this incremental: what state must carry over from one hour's run to the next, and how do you handle a SUSPEND that arrives late?

rules.ask: With LEAD from each RESUME to the next event, what happens when a RESIZE, or a second RESUME, sits between it and its SUSPEND?
A run lasts from 10:40 to 12:15. If you truncate only its start to the hour, where do its 95 minutes go? How do you split it?
Two runs resume 30 seconds apart and each lasts 10 seconds. Is your minimum per run, or per warehouse and minute, and what would the bill say?
Do you round per run or per hour? Show what 3,600 separate one-second X-Small charges round to each way.
You merged overlapping billed intervals. Is that what the billing rule says, and what does it do to two minimums that overlap?

incidents: A monitoring probe resumes one of {{warehouse_list}} every 70 seconds for a one-second query, and auto-suspend stops it in between; each resume pays its own 60-second minimum, and this report shows the idle warehouse costing more than the busiest one.

A run of this report up to {{report_end}} disagreed with a rerun the next morning for the same hours: runs open at report_end were billed only up to it, and SUSPEND events still arriving late moved seconds between hours. Finance numbers should come only from hours closed after the log's delay.

templates.title: Secure data sharing across accounts and regions
templates.subtopic: grants, entitlements, cross-region replication, revocation

sections.scenario: A cloud data platform lets a provider account give other accounts live, read-only access to some of its databases without copying them: within one region, a share is a set of grants on the provider's stored data, and consumers query it with their own compute and pay for that compute. A data provider sells {{shared_tb}} of market and reference data to {{consumers}} consumer accounts in {{regions}} regions across more than one cloud. Some consumers are entitled to every row; others only to some markets or tiers. Consumers in other regions must see the provider's updates within {{refresh}}. When a contract ends, access must stop everywhere.
sections.problem: Design the sharing capability as the provider experiences it: the grant model (what a share contains and who may use it), how per-consumer row entitlements are enforced, how data reaches consumers in other regions, how revocation works in every region, and the audit trail of who could read what and who did. Say what is copied, where, and who pays for it.
sections.constraints: No copy of the data within a region. Remote regions see updates within {{refresh}}. Revocation takes effect within one minute in every region, including regions served from a replica. The provider never sees consumers' query text. A consumer can never see another consumer's rows, the provider's unshared objects, or the definition of the views that filter its rows. Every grant change and every access is auditable for two years.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and timings are hypothetical. This exercise's rule: data does not cross regions at query time; to serve a consumer in another region, the provider replicates the shared database into an account it owns in that region and shares it from there (check current docs). The platform's storage is immutable files; any change writes new files.
sections.criteria: Separates control plane (grants and entitlements checked at query time, revocation propagated independently of data refresh) from data plane (no in-region copies, replication of changed files to provider-owned accounts in remote regions); row entitlements through a secure view and an entitlement table keyed by an immutable account identifier, with the view definition hidden; a cost model for replication based on changed bytes, with a plan for rewrite-heavy operations; precise revocation semantics including running queries, caches and replicas; an audit trail of grant changes and object-level access without consumer query text; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a consumer in another region query the provider's primary region directly?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; data is replicated into the consumer's region first, and the transfer is the provider's cost.

clarifications.q: Who pays for what?
clarifications.a: Consumers pay for their query compute; the provider pays for storage, replication compute and data transfer.

clarifications.q: What happens to a query that is running when access is revoked?
clarifications.a: Your call; say what you choose and why.

clarifications.q: Are entitlements per table or per row?
clarifications.a: Both: some consumers get whole tables, others a subset of rows by market and tier, and the subset changes when a contract is amended.

clarifications.q: Can consumers copy shared data into their own tables?
clarifications.a: Yes, once they can read it. Revocation cannot claw copies back; contracts cover that.

hints: Separate the control plane (who may read what, decided centrally and checked at query time) from the data plane (where the bytes live). Revocation belongs to the control plane.
Per-consumer row subsets are easier to run as one secure view joined to an entitlement table keyed by the querying account than as hundreds of separate shares.
Replication ships changed immutable files. Estimate a day's changed bytes, not the size of the whole database, and ask what makes that number jump.
followups: Walk through what happens, end to end, the first time a consumer in a remote region queries a table the provider added to the share an hour ago.
A contract ends at midnight. What exactly stops working, where, and how quickly, in the primary region and in each of the {{regions}} regions?
How do you enforce row entitlements so a consumer can neither see other consumers' rows nor learn the filter from the view?
Replicating {{shared_tb}} to {{regions}} regions is the provider's largest bill. How do you cut it without breaking the {{refresh}} promise?
An auditor asks which consumer accounts could read one table on one day last year, and which actually did. How do you answer, and how do you prove it?

rules.ask: You send some consumers an extract. Who owns that copy, how fresh is it, and what does a revocation do to it?
A revocation is made in the primary region one minute after the last replication refresh. What does the consumer in a replica region see until the next refresh?
Your entitlement table is keyed by the consumer's account name, and the consumer's account is renamed in a migration. What does that consumer see, and what would a new account with the old name see?
The provider asks for the text of the queries a consumer ran against their data. What do you give them, and why?
A consumer's dashboard is answered from a cached result after its access was revoked. Is that a breach in your design?

incidents: A contract ends and the provider removes the consumer from the share. In the primary region the consumer's queries fail within seconds, but in one of the {{regions}} regions the consumer keeps reading for up to {{refresh}}, because the replicated database carried the grants with the data and the removal only arrived with the next refresh.

The provider re-clusters its largest table, rewriting every file. The next replication refresh tries to send most of the {{shared_tb}} to every region; refreshes overrun {{refresh}} for two days and the week's data transfer bill triples.

The entitlement table behind a secure view is keyed by consumer account name. After one consumer's account is renamed in an organisation migration, the consumer sees an empty table for a day and opens a support case; nobody had noticed that a new account created with the old name would have matched its rows.

templates.title: Micro-partition metadata, pruning statistics and automatic reclustering
templates.subtopic: file statistics, partition pruning, clustering depth, background reclustering

sections.scenario: An analytical engine stores every table as immutable columnar files, called micro-partitions here, each holding tens to a few hundred megabytes of rows; any insert, update or delete writes new files and retires old ones. Before a query runs, the compiler decides which files to read from statistics kept for every file and column. One tenant's largest table is {{table_size}}, grows by {{ingest}}, and most of its queries filter on {{filter_col}}, usually for a narrow range. The tenant may declare a clustering key; without one, files are in load order.
sections.problem: Design the metadata layer: which statistics are captured per file and column, how they are written with each commit, where they are stored and how the compiler reads them at this scale, the pruning rules (which predicates can use which statistics), a clustering-quality metric (overlap and depth), and an automatic reclustering service that keeps pruning effective while spending no more than {{recluster_budget}} of the tenant's query compute.
sections.constraints: Pruning must never skip a file that holds a matching row: reading too many files is acceptable, missing a row is not. Metadata time at compile is under 500 ms at p95 even for a table with tens of millions of files. Statistics are committed atomically with the files they describe. Reclustering never blocks loads or queries, and its compute appears on the tenant's bill.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, rates and budgets are hypothetical. This exercise's rule: a micro-partition holds 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data (check current docs). The metadata store is a separate service from file storage and can be scaled independently.
sections.criteria: Per-file, per-column statistics (minimum, maximum, null count, optionally distinct estimates) committed atomically with the files; a metadata store organised so compile reads only the columns and ranges it needs (sorted or interval-indexed by the clustering key, tiered caching); conservative pruning rules that are provably correct for truncated strings, NULLs and expressions; a precise clustering depth or overlap metric maintained incrementally; a reclustering service with a cost model, a budget, and policies for hot recent ranges; awareness of rewrite costs on history and replicas; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which statistics exist per column?
clarifications.a: You choose. At least minimum, maximum and null count; say what else earns its space.

clarifications.q: How are long strings handled?
clarifications.a: Long strings are common (URLs, paths, JSON keys). You decide how much of each value the statistics keep, and must keep pruning correct.

clarifications.q: Do queries filter with expressions, such as a cast to date or LIKE 'abc%'?
clarifications.a: Yes, often. Say which predicates can use the statistics and which cannot.

clarifications.q: Are loads ordered by the filter column?
clarifications.a: Usually close to it, but some loading tools write in arbitrary order.

clarifications.q: Can reclustering run while loads continue?
clarifications.a: It must. A load and a recluster may touch the same files.

hints: Pruning is a containment test: a file can be skipped only if its [min, max] for the column cannot contain any value the predicate accepts. Work out what that requires for truncated strings and for NULLs.
Clustering depth: for a point in the key's range, how many files overlap it. Its average over the range tells you how much a narrow filter has to read.
Reclustering rewrites files, and everything that keeps files (time travel history, replicas, caches) pays for each rewrite. Spend the budget where benefit per byte rewritten is highest.
followups: A query filters {{filter_col}} to one day. Walk through how the compiler goes from the predicate to a list of files, and how many metadata rows it touches.
Statistics truncate strings to save space. How do you store minimum and maximum so pruning stays correct?
Define clustering depth precisely, and say how you maintain it incrementally as {{ingest}} of new files arrives.
Which files does the reclustering service choose each cycle, and how do you show the tenant it was worth {{recluster_budget}} of their compute?
The table is joined to a small dimension filtered on one region. How could pruning use the join, not only literal predicates?

rules.ask: Files are immutable and written by the thousand every minute. What does maintaining that index cost per load, and what does it buy over per-file minimum and maximum?
How large is each file's filter at this column's cardinality, and for which predicates does it help where minimum and maximum do not?
A file's largest URL shares its first 32 bytes with the value in the predicate. Show me the stored maximum and why that file is not wrongly skipped.
Loads arrive every minute. Do you re-sort the whole table? If not, what bounds the overlap between new files and old ones?
The table has tens of millions of files and one column's statistics do not fit in one compiler's memory. What do you load, and when?

incidents: A tenant switches to a loading tool that writes rows in arbitrary order of {{filter_col}}. Within a week nearly every new file spans most of the column's range, pruning for one-day queries falls from 99% of files skipped to 3%, and their warehouses run ten times longer.

A release truncates string statistics to 16 bytes and stores the truncated value as the maximum. Queries that filter on long string keys silently miss rows from some files; a customer's reconciliation finds 0.2% of rows missing before anyone suspects the engine.

With a steady trickle of {{ingest}}, the reclustering service rewrites the same recent range over and over. It spends three times its {{recluster_budget}} budget, depth barely improves, and time-travel storage grows with every rewrite.

templates.title: Query result cache and materialised-view freshness service
templates.subtopic: result caching, cache keys and invalidation, incremental view maintenance

sections.scenario: Business intelligence dashboards across many tenants of a cloud data platform send the same aggregate queries again and again: {{dashboards}} dashboards produce {{qps}} queries per second at peak, and most are identical to a query that ran minutes earlier. Base tables receive loads every {{load_interval}}. Tenants also define materialised views over their largest tables, maintained in the background at their cost, and expect queries on the base table to be answered from a view when that is faster. A view-answered result must be {{staleness}}.
sections.problem: Design two things that work together. First, a query result cache that returns a stored result without running the query, whenever that result is still exactly what the query would return now for this user. Second, a freshness service for materialised views: how views are kept current, how a query against a base table is rewritten to use a view, and how the engine decides per query whether the view is fresh enough. Cover keys, invalidation, security, storage limits and cost.
sections.constraints: A cached result must never reach a user who could not see exactly that result now (privileges, row access policies, masking policies). Results from the cache must equal a fresh execution; queries with non-deterministic functions are never served from it. View-answered results must be {{staleness}}. Cache storage is bounded per tenant, and one tenant's results are never visible to another.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and rates are hypothetical. This exercise's rule: a stored result is kept for 24 hours after its last use, each reuse extends that, up to 31 days after the first run (check current docs). Every commit to a table produces a new table version.
sections.criteria: A cache key that includes normalised text, table versions, effective security policy versions and semantic session settings; detection of non-deterministic functions; version-based validity instead of timed expiry; tenant isolation and bounded storage with an eviction policy; incremental view maintenance with clear rules for which aggregates allow it and how deletes are handled; a per-query decision to use the view, the view plus base deltas, or the base table, honouring the staleness bound; cost accounting that compares maintenance with savings; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Must the query text match exactly?
clarifications.a: You decide how much normalisation to do; say what could go wrong with each step.

clarifications.q: Are queries using the current timestamp or random sampling cacheable?
clarifications.a: Say which functions make a query uncacheable and how the engine detects them.

clarifications.q: Can two users share one cached result?
clarifications.a: Only when both may see exactly that result. You define what that takes.

clarifications.q: Do session settings such as time zone vary?
clarifications.a: Yes, per session, and some change query results.

clarifications.q: Who pays for view maintenance?
clarifications.a: The tenant, as background compute shown separately on the bill.

hints: A cache key is everything the result depends on: the normalised query, the version of every table read, the effective security policies, and the session settings that change semantics.
If every commit makes a new table version, a cached entry is valid exactly while the versions it read are still current; no invalidation messages are needed.
A view can answer an "always current" query by combining the view with the base table's changes since its last refresh, when the aggregate allows it.
followups: Two analysts with different roles run the same dashboard query. Walk through the cache lookup for each.
Base tables change every {{load_interval}}. What hit rate do you expect, and what could product or engine change to raise it?
How does the freshness service decide when to refresh a view, and what happens to a query that arrives when the view is behind?
Which aggregates can be maintained incrementally and which force a recompute? Treat COUNT(DISTINCT), MIN and MAX, and deletes.
How do you show a tenant that the cache and their views save more compute than the views cost?

rules.ask: Two queries differ only in a comment, or in the case of a string literal. Which normalisations are safe, and which change the result?
A load lands one second after a result is cached with a 10-minute expiry. What does the next user get?
The table is shared from another account, and the provider changes it there. How does the consumer's cache learn about it?
A masking policy on an email column changes, but no table data changes. Does your cache key notice?
A delete removes rows from the base table. How does the view's MAX(amount) per day stay correct?

incidents: A row access policy is tightened for one region's analysts. For the next several hours some of them still see rows they may no longer read, served from results cached before the change; the policy's version was not part of the cache key.

Analysts in a time zone ahead of UTC see yesterday's totals on a dashboard at 00:30 local time: the cache key ignored the session time zone and served a result that a user in another zone had computed with a different "today".

A bulk correction updates 30% of a large base table. Its view falls behind, every dashboard query that used the view now runs on the base table at {{qps}} queries per second, and the warehouse queue grows for an hour.

templates.title: Time travel and fail-safe retention architecture
templates.subtopic: table versions, undrop and clones, garbage collection, retention cost

sections.scenario: A cloud data platform stores every table as immutable files and a sequence of table versions. Users can query a table as it was at an earlier time or before a given statement, restore dropped tables, schemas and databases with UNDROP, and clone a table, schema or database at a point in time without copying files. Time-travel retention is set per object, here {{retention_days}} days. After it ends, data passes into a fail-safe period that users cannot query and only the platform's operators can recover from. One customer account holds {{tables}} tables and {{storage}} of active data; on a typical day {{churn}} of the rows in its busiest tables are rewritten by updates, deletes, or truncate-and-reload jobs.
sections.problem: Design the retention architecture: table-version metadata, how a time-travel query resolves a timestamp or statement to files, how UNDROP and clones work, garbage collection that deletes a file only when nothing can need it again, storage accounting per table per day split into active, time-travel and fail-safe bytes, and how the customer sees and controls the cost.
sections.constraints: A file is deleted only when no version inside any retention or fail-safe window and no clone references it. Garbage collection is safe under concurrent commits, clones and crashes. Time travel adds little compile overhead. Retention changes take effect predictably and are explained to the customer. The storage report is available per table per day.
sections.assumptions: All sizes and counts are hypothetical. This exercise's rules: time-travel retention can be 0 to 90 days depending on the object and the account's edition, and fail-safe is 7 days after retention for permanent tables, with none for transient and temporary tables (check current docs).
sections.criteria: Versions as immutable file lists with commit times and statement ids; time-travel resolution by version lookup; UNDROP as restoring a dropped object's version chain with a clear name-conflict rule; clones as shared file references; garbage collection by reachability across all tables and clones (or crash-safe reference counts), with a grace period and an audit of deletions; storage accounting by state with attribution for shared files; customer-facing controls (transient tables, shorter retention for staging data, alerts on history-to-active ratio); an honest account of deletion requests versus retention; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: What happens to history when retention is shortened?
clarifications.a: You decide whether it is deleted now or ages out; say what the customer is told.

clarifications.q: Does a clone copy files?
clarifications.a: No. A clone references the source's files, and the two diverge as either changes.

clarifications.q: Can a user drop a table, create a new one with the same name, then UNDROP the old one?
clarifications.a: Users will try; say what happens.

clarifications.q: Who pays for fail-safe bytes?
clarifications.a: The customer; they appear on the bill as fail-safe storage.

clarifications.q: Are row deletes physically applied?
clarifications.a: Files are immutable. A delete writes new files without the rows and retires the old ones.

hints: A table version is a list of files and a commit time; time travel is a lookup of the newest version at or before the requested point.
A file lives from the version that adds it until the version that retires it, plus retention, plus fail-safe, but clones can extend that. Think about reference counts or reachability across tables.

Attribute bytes by state: active while the current version uses a file, time travel while only history inside retention does, fail-safe after that. Decide who is charged for a file a clone still uses.
followups: Walk through a query AT a timestamp three days ago: which metadata is read and which files are scanned.
Show how garbage collection decides a file can go when the table has been cloned twice and the source then dropped.
A table is truncated and reloaded daily with {{retention_days}}-day retention. Estimate its time-travel and fail-safe bytes relative to its active bytes, and say what you would tell the customer.
How does UNDROP of a whole schema with thousands of tables work, including name conflicts?
A data subject's rows must be gone within 30 days of a request. How does that interact with time travel and fail-safe, and what do you offer?

rules.ask: Is each of your snapshots a copy of the data or a list of files? What would a daily snapshot of {{storage}} cost in your design?
Garbage collection crashes after decrementing a count and before deleting the file. What happens on restart, and can it ever delete a live file?
Compaction rewrites small files into large ones. What does it do to time-travel storage for the next {{retention_days}} days?
How long does the tombstone live, and what reclaims the space of a dropped table that is never undropped?
The rows are gone from the current version but still inside time travel and fail-safe. What do you tell the requester, and when are they really gone?

incidents: A customer's jobs truncate and reload its biggest tables every day. With {{retention_days}}-day retention, the time-travel and fail-safe bytes of those tables reach many times their active bytes and the month's storage bill jumps. The customer asks why nothing warned them.

A release changes garbage collection to compute reachability per table. Files still used by a clone whose source table was dropped are deleted when the source's retention ends, and queries on the clone fail with missing-file errors.
A user drops a production schema by mistake. UNDROP fails for 40 of its tables because an automated job had already created new tables with the same names a few minutes later.

templates.title: Marketplace listing analytics without exposing consumers' queries
templates.subtopic: access records, aggregation thresholds, differencing, restatement

sections.scenario: A data marketplace lets {{providers}} providers publish {{listings}} listings: free, trial and paid datasets that consumers in other accounts obtain through data sharing and query with their own compute. Providers want analytics: how many accounts viewed a listing, requested it or obtained it, how many trials converted to paid, which shared objects and columns consumers use and how often, and which consumer accounts are active. Consumers expect that a provider never sees their query text, the values they filter on, or what they do with data they copied, and that browsing by accounts that never obtained the listing is shown only in aggregate. Providers expect numbers no older than {{freshness}}.
sections.problem: Design the analytics pipeline, the provider-facing data model, the privacy rules and how providers access the results. Say which raw records you use, how they become daily facts, what each provider can and cannot see, how small groups are protected, and how late or replayed records change published numbers.
sections.constraints: Query text and literal values never reach provider-facing data. Browsing activity is published only in aggregate, and any group of fewer than {{min_group}} distinct accounts is suppressed. Consumers who obtained a listing are identified to its provider by account and organisation (this exercise's rule: the provider already has a contract or request from them). A provider sees only its own listings. Restatements are allowed but announced.
sections.assumptions: All counts and timings are hypothetical. Each consumer query against shared data produces an access record listing the shared objects and columns it read, separate from the query's text, which stays in the consumer's own history.
sections.criteria: Facts derived from object-access records with no query text or literals; separate identified-usage and anonymous-browsing models with different rules; minimum group size applied to distinct accounts plus protection against differencing (fixed published cuts, coarse dimensions, suppression of complementary cells, or noise where exactness is not needed, with exact metrics kept for billing); idempotent ingestion keyed by access-record id; a stated restatement policy with versioned daily partitions and notices; delivery to providers as shared tables scoped to their listings; a data-minimisation review gate on any new field; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can the provider see which columns a consumer read?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, at object and column level, counted per day; never the query text, its predicates or the consumer's own tables it joined.

clarifications.q: Are individual user names shown?
clarifications.a: No, account and organisation level only.

clarifications.q: What about consumers who copy shared data into their own tables?
clarifications.a: The copy is theirs; activity on it is not visible to the provider.

clarifications.q: How do providers get the analytics?
clarifications.a: As tables shared into their own account, queried with their own compute.

clarifications.q: Is the minimum group size a legal requirement?
clarifications.a: It is this product's policy; you may propose a different number with reasons.

hints: Build provider-facing facts from object-access records (which shared objects and columns a query touched), never from query text.
A minimum group size alone does not stop a provider subtracting one aggregate from another. Think about differencing across filters, listings and days.
Identified usage (accounts that obtained the listing) and anonymous browsing need different rules; keep them in different tables.
followups: Define the daily fact tables providers query: grain, keys, and which columns come from which raw source.
A provider narrows the browsing view to one region and one industry where only a handful of accounts viewed the listing. What do they learn, and what stops it?
How do you count trial-to-paid conversion when consumer accounts merge or move between organisations?
Access records from one region arrive two days late. How do published numbers change, and how do providers find out?
A provider asks for the most common filter values used against their table, to improve the product. What can you safely offer?

rules.ask: Even with literals stripped, the shape of a query can reveal intent. Which fields of a query ever reach provider-facing data in your design?
The provider changes a filter so two groups that both clear the threshold differ by exactly one account. How does your design stop the subtraction?
Providers reconcile billing against some of these numbers. Which metrics get noise, and which must be exact?
What is the key of one access record, and what happens when a region replays a day of records?
Does the provider's dashboard run on the provider's compute or the platform's, and who can see the provider's own queries against it?

incidents: A provider compares listing views for "financial services, all regions" with "financial services, all regions except one". Both groups clear the {{min_group}}-account threshold, but they differ by one account, and the provider learns that a specific competitor browsed its listing.

A logging change starts attaching the first 200 characters of query text to access records for debugging. The text reaches provider-facing tables for several providers and stays there for three {{freshness}} refresh cycles before anyone notices.

Access records from one region are replayed after a pipeline fault and one day's usage counts double for listings in that region. Providers who bill their own consumers by usage send invoices on the inflated numbers.

templates.title: Blameless review when an executive wants a name after a sharing misconfiguration
templates.subtopic: blameless review, accountability, executive communication

exposure: one consumer account could read two other consumers' rows through a shared view for six hours
a share meant for a trial consumer granted the full paid dataset for nine days
a test listing exposed a table of customer contract prices to three outside accounts for a day
exec: the head of the business unit that owns the dataset

sections.scenario: Your team publishes your company's datasets to customers through a cloud data platform's data sharing and marketplace. Last week {{exposure}}. A customer noticed and reported it; access was removed within the hour of the report, and the affected customers have been told. The change that caused it was made by an engineer on your team following the documented process, and two colleagues approved it in review. Two levels above you, {{exec}} has told you in front of others that they want to know "who did this" and expects a name in the review within {{days}} days.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover confirming the exposure is fully contained and understood, how you run the review, what you say to {{exec}} and when, how you support the engineer, what accountability looks like in your answer, which actions come out of it and how you know they worked. Then tell me about a real incident review you led or took part in where blame was in the air, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Legal and the customer-facing team are involved and need facts, not opinions. The engineer is upset and has offered to resign. You cannot delay the review past {{days}} days.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Confirms containment from evidence (access history, other shares with the same pattern) before anything else; runs a blameless review that traces the failure to process and system gaps (no automated entitlement check, an ignored near miss) and names owners for fixes, including their own; answers the executive promptly and directly, declines to make the review about a name while offering accountability, a timeline and measurable actions; supports the engineer privately and publicly; actions are verifiable and followed up; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Was the documented process followed?
clarifications.a: Yes. It had no automated check that a shared view's filter matched each consumer's entitlement.

clarifications.q: Has this kind of change gone wrong before?
clarifications.a: A near miss six months ago was caught in review; nothing changed afterwards.

clarifications.q: Does the executive have authority over the engineer's employment?
clarifications.a: Not directly; your manager and HR do. But the executive's view carries weight.

clarifications.q: Do you know exactly what was read?
clarifications.a: Access history shows which accounts queried which objects and when; you have not yet checked it in detail.

hints: First make sure the facts are complete: who could read what, who did, for how long, and whether anything else shares the same flaw.
Accountability in a blameless review is for the system and its owners, including you, not the absence of accountability.
Give the executive what they actually need: confidence that it is understood, contained and will not recur, with dates.
followups: What do you check in the first day to be sure the exposure is contained and nothing similar is still open?
How do you answer {{exec}} when they ask for the name, and what do you offer them instead?
What does the review conclude about why two reviewers and a documented process let this through?
Six weeks later, how do you know the actions worked, and who would tell you if they had not?
In your real example, what did the review change, and how did the person closest to the mistake fare afterwards?

rules.ask: What would that action teach the next engineer who finds a mistake like this in their own change?
The executive says "blameless means nobody is accountable." What do you answer, and who is accountable in your account?
Which of your "whys" ends at a person, and how do you continue past it?
The check you propose would have caught this case. Which class of sharing mistake does it still miss?
What did you personally say to the executive, and when?

templates.title: Consolidating three orchestration tools across the organisation
templates.subtopic: migration strategy, adoption across teams, decommissioning

tools: a self-hosted open-source workflow scheduler, cron jobs on virtual machines and the warehouse's own scheduled tasks
two open-source workflow schedulers on different major versions and a commercial ELT tool's scheduler
the warehouse's own scheduled tasks, a managed workflow service and a scheduler written in-house years ago

sections.scenario: Your organisation loads data into and out of a cloud data warehouse with {{pipelines}} scheduled pipelines owned by {{teams}} teams, orchestrated by {{tools}}. Dependencies between tools are expressed as schedules ("run at 03:15 because that one usually finishes by 03:00"); three of last quarter's incidents started when an upstream job ran late and a downstream job read half-loaded tables. Nobody can list every pipeline with its owner. You have been asked to lead a consolidation and to show progress within {{months}} months.
sections.problem: How would you lead it? Cover how you decide whether to consolidate and onto what, the evidence you gather first, the migration plan, how you get {{teams}} teams to move while they have their own roadmaps, what you choose not to migrate, how you measure success, and how the old tools are switched off. Then tell me about a real platform migration or consolidation you led or took part in, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You have three engineers for the work and no authority over the other teams' plans. Some pipelines feed external customers through data shares, and their timing is promised. The old tools' licences and machines cost money every month they stay up.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Starts with an inventory and the failure that matters (missing explicit dependencies); chooses the target on criteria tied to that failure (dependency modelling, retries and backfills, observability, cost, skills) and considers keeping more than one tool where justified; a phased plan (stop new pipelines on old tools, make the new path easier, migrate by dependency cluster, high-risk last or with dual running and output comparison); wins teams through reduced work and clear support rather than only mandate, with escalation where needed; retires orphan pipelines safely (switch off with notice, watch for complaints); measurable outcomes (incidents, pipelines migrated, cost retired); real example with personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the target tool already chosen?
clarifications.a: No. Leadership expects a recommendation from you.

clarifications.q: Do teams want this?
clarifications.a: Some do; others say their tool works fine and migration is risk with no benefit to them.

clarifications.q: Are there pipelines without an owner?
clarifications.a: Probably; nobody has checked.

clarifications.q: Can you block new pipelines on the old tools?
clarifications.a: You can propose it; your director would have to agree.

hints: An inventory comes first: every pipeline, its owner, its schedule, what it reads and writes, and what depends on it.
The problem in last quarter's incidents was missing dependencies, not the number of tools; make sure your target fixes that.
Make the new path easier than the old one before asking anyone to move, and stop the old path from growing.
followups: How do you build the inventory, and what do you do about pipelines nobody owns?
How do you choose the target, and what would make you recommend keeping two tools instead of one?
A team with a fifth of all pipelines refuses to migrate this year. What do you do?
How do you migrate the pipelines behind customer-facing shares without missing their promised times?
In your real example, what did you underestimate, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: The director mandates the move by a date. Which teams miss it, and what happens to their pipelines then?
Which pipelines move first, and what is your rollback if a migrated pipeline produces different numbers?
How many of the {{pipelines}} pipelines need a rewrite rather than a translation, and who pays for that time?
Your inventory finds a fifth of pipelines with no owner. Which do you switch off, and how do you find out who needed them?
Which decision was yours, and who disagreed?

templates.title: A VP's urgent request against the team's committed quarter
templates.subtopic: competing commitments, saying no with options, stakeholder management

request: a usage dashboard for a large prospect evaluating your data listings, to be shown in their final review
per-customer warehouse spend reports that finance wants before budget season
a new curated dataset shared with a strategic partner for a joint announcement
committed: moving the ingestion pipeline off a loader that is being retired
row-level entitlements for every shared dataset
rebuilding the shared reporting tables as incremental models

sections.scenario: Halfway through the quarter, a VP who is not in your management chain asks your team directly for {{request}} within {{weeks}} weeks. Your team is committed to {{committed}}, which two other teams depend on, and the plan has no slack. Your manager is on leave this week. The VP says the request is "the top priority for the company" and has already told the prospect or partner it will happen.
sections.problem: What do you do this week, and over the next {{weeks}} weeks? Cover how you understand what is really needed and by when, how you estimate it honestly, what options you put on the table and what each costs the committed work and the teams depending on it, who decides, how you communicate with the VP, your manager and the dependent teams, and what you do if the decision goes against your team's plan. Then tell me about a real time an urgent request collided with committed work, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot add people this quarter. The dependent teams have their own commitments built on yours. Saying yes to everything means missing something.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clarifies the underlying need, deadline and smallest sufficient version before committing; estimates honestly; offers options with explicit costs to committed work and dependent teams; routes the decision to the person who owns both priorities, with the manager informed despite leave; communicates the decision in writing to the VP, the team and dependent teams; protects the team from unsustainable overtime; handles repeat requests with a lightweight intake rule; real example with the trade-off made and its outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the VP's claim about company priority true?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet. Nobody has written it down.

clarifications.q: Could another team do it?
clarifications.a: Possibly a smaller version; they are also busy.

clarifications.q: Can you reach your manager?
clarifications.a: By message, with a delay of a day or two.

clarifications.q: What is the smallest useful version?
clarifications.a: You have not asked yet.

hints: Ask what decision or event the request serves; that sets the real deadline and the smallest version that is enough.
Turn the conflict into options with costs, not a yes or a no.
The decision belongs to whoever owns both priorities; get it made in writing and tell everyone affected.
followups: What do you ask the VP in your first conversation?
Lay out the options you would offer and what each costs the committed work.
The decision is to do the request in full and delay the committed work by {{weeks}} weeks. What do you tell the two dependent teams, and when?
The VP comes back a week later with a second urgent request. What do you do differently?
In your real example, what did you give up, and was it worth it in hindsight?

rules.ask: The VP replies that "no" is not an option and they will take it to your director. What do you do next?
For how many weeks can the team keep that up, and what does it cost you next quarter?
What exactly do you put in front of the person who decides, and how do you present the VP's case fairly?
Which part of the request does your smaller version leave out, and has the VP agreed it is enough?
What did you personally recommend, and to whom?

templates.title: Setting a freshness objective with product for a feature that never had one
templates.subtopic: defining freshness, cost of options, agreement with product

feature: the consumer usage charts that data providers see for their listings
a customer-facing dashboard of warehouse spend by team
a popularity signal used to rank marketplace listings in search
lag: anything from 5 minutes to a full day

sections.scenario: Your team's pipelines feed {{feature}}. Nobody has ever said how fresh its data must be. Measured from the moment an event happens to the moment it shows in the feature, the lag is {{lag}}. Support logged {{complaints}} complaints about stale data last quarter. The product manager wants it "real time"; your engineers say the pipeline is a batch job on a schedule and real time would be a rebuild. You have been asked to agree a freshness objective with product and then make it true.
sections.problem: How would you lead this? Cover how you define freshness precisely (which timestamps, measured where, at what percentile, over what window), how you find out what users actually need, how you cost each option, how you reach agreement with product, how you instrument and publish it, what happens when the objective is missed, and how it is reviewed. Then tell me about a real time you set a reliability or freshness objective with a partner team, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The team has one quarter and no extra headcount. The warehouse budget for the pipeline can grow by at most a third. Product owns the feature's promises to customers.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Measures the current lag end to end and per stage with a distribution; defines freshness precisely (event time to visible time, at a percentile over a window, with a stated handling of late and restated data); grounds the requirement in user decisions rather than labels; costs options in money and effort (more frequent batches, micro-batches, incremental processing, streaming) within the budget; reaches a written agreement with product including what customers are told; instruments and publishes freshness in the feature itself, with alerts, an owner and an agreed response when missed; reviews it periodically; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is any promise already made to customers?
clarifications.a: The documentation says "updated regularly". Sales have said "near real time" in some calls.

clarifications.q: Where does the lag come from today?
clarifications.a: You have not broken it down; the pipeline has four stages and one of them is a daily job.

clarifications.q: What do the complaints say?
clarifications.a: Mostly that numbers changed after a decision was made on them, or that today's activity was missing.

clarifications.q: Who would be paged if the objective were missed?
clarifications.a: Nobody today.

hints: Measure before negotiating: where the lag comes from, stage by stage, and how it is distributed, not just its average.
Ask what decision users make with the feature and how fast that decision needs new data; that is the requirement, not "real time".
An objective needs an owner, a measurement users can see, and an agreed response when it is missed.
followups: Define the freshness measure you would propose, precisely enough that two engineers would compute the same number.
What options would you cost for product, and what does each cost in money and team time?
Product insists on five minutes. The cheapest design that meets it would double the warehouse spend. What happens next?
The objective is agreed. Two months later it is missed for three days running. What happens, and who decides?
In your real example, how did the objective change behaviour on both teams?

rules.ask: Which decision does a user make differently with data that is seconds old rather than fifteen minutes old?
Measured over what window, from which timestamp, and what does a user see when a day falls outside it?
Who gets paged at 03:00 when freshness slips, and what can they actually do about it?
Is this promised to customers or only internal? Who decides, and what changes if it is promised?
Which part of the agreement was your proposal, and what did product change in it?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for multi-tenant elastic compute
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, workload isolation and elastic compute

angle: the workload that was hardest to keep fast
the decision that most changed what the system cost
the failure that taught you the most
tenant_feature: separate compute per tenant that suspends when idle and resumes on the next query
a spending limit per tenant with alerts and a hard stop
isolation so that one tenant's heavy jobs never slow the others

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if it served many tenants on elastic compute, the way a cloud data platform runs each workload on warehouses that can be resized, scaled out and suspended, at {{scale}} today's load, and with {{tenant_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at {{scale}} the load, with tenants sharing the system, and with {{tenant_feature}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear which parts you are recalling and which you are reasoning through.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The multi-tenant, elastic setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers (peak and average, data size, latency or freshness targets, cost); depth on the chosen angle down to workloads, keys and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a scaling analysis that names the first bottleneck and how it would be seen early; a concrete, incremental path to the tenant feature with its new failure modes (resume latency, hard stops interrupting critical jobs, isolation cost); own contribution separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a data system?
clarifications.a: It should move, store or compute data others depend on; a service with a significant data model counts.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to workloads, keys, failure modes, costs and numbers.

clarifications.q: Does "elastic" mean I must have used a cloud warehouse?
clarifications.a: No. Reason about compute that can be added, removed and paused, whatever you used.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers, including peak against average, before the architecture.
Know what each workload in your system costs and what it competes with for resources.
For the elastic question, decide what is shared (storage, metadata, compute) and what each tenant gets of its own.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
At {{scale}} the load, which component fails first, and how would you know before users did?
How would you add {{tenant_feature}} without a rewrite, and what new failure does it bring?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
What signal triggers scaling, how long does new capacity take to help, and what do queries do in the meantime?
How long did queries wait at peak, and who decided that was acceptable?
How much did the system cost per month, which workload drove it, and what did you change because of it?
One tenant is a hundred times larger than the median. Where in your design does their load stop affecting the others?
